# Work list

Everything left before Olo is complete and everything finished, in five
parts (Ben, 2026-11-06): what is being worked on now, what isn't started
yet (highest priority first), what is done but waits for Ben to try or
confirm, what is blocked (on Ben, a person at the machine, hardware or
data), and what is finished, most recently finished first. Keep it
current: an item moves part to part as it goes, and when it lands it is
struck (with the commit) and moved to the top of Finished; a new one
goes where its state and priority put it. An item that is done but has
a "Left" for Ben is in "Waiting for Ben"; one whose next step needs
something nobody here has is in "Blocked", with what it waits for.

## Not started (highest priority first)

- **Nothing may hold the desktop up, whatever the load: the GPU's
  resets, the desktop's place on the GPU, the kernel's own threads**
  (Ben, 2026-11-20: "something is really broken my desktop is lagging
  … deskbar keeps crashing"; "why are they so impactful? those
  headless sessions and agent screens should be super efficient … i
  don't want you to just limit concurrency i want it to work more
  efficiently"; "whatever you find don't just fix it for me right now
  manually, you need to fix the root cause and make sure none of this
  will happen again in olo"; "the desktop responsiveness must never
  suffer no matter the load"; "if you need to write a new kernel
  module as part of olo … that's also on the table if it can't be
  done through standard linux mechanisms. if you do that, work with
  astra 6.2 max on the design and implementation and review"). Three
  causes, each measured (HACKING, "The GPU has priorities too"):
  1. **The freezes of seconds, and programs starting again, were
     GPU resets Olo brought on itself.** Since 2026-11-15 every
     headless app_server asked the GPU's lowest priority, and kit
     programs on agents' screens too. Intel's firmware scheduler
     gives such a queue nothing while any ordinary one has work
     (measured: a 0.2 ms draw waited 2012 ms beside one ordinary
     program busy for 2.0 s; 12 ms at the ordinary priority), and xe
     (Linux 7.2) resets the whole GPU when a job has waited five
     seconds to start (`check_timeout`, read in the kernel's source;
     all fifteen resets that day began with a headless app_server's
     job "not started"; the second investigator decoded the dump: no
     hung job, no full channel). Each reset then timed out up to
     fifteen other programs' work: their devices lost, the kit
     starting them again, the person's screen still meanwhile. The
     trigger each time was a push's live lint (a dozen desktops
     drawing at once). **Done**: nothing of Olo's asks for less than
     the ordinary priority (`headless::gpu_priority`, a test; the
     kit's and blade's low queue removed), seen from the kernel (a
     headless compositor and a kit program on an agent's screen both
     ask 1, normal); `tools/dev/gpu-priority-check` measures it again
     (guarded: two seconds, never near the five). **Left**: (a)
     ~~agents' screens started before the upgrade keep their low
     queues until they start again: do they start again at an
     upgrade?~~ they do (seen 2026-11-20: a screen started at 23:04
     had its compositor started again at 23:26:36, five seconds
     after the person's, at that night's upgrade: its session is an
     `olo-session --headless` and re-executes as the person's does);
     (b) ~~the root follower sets the
     driver's patience to its most (`job_timeout_ms`, 10 s, for
     queues made after) for other programs' low queues~~ done
     (`gpu_tuning::xe_patience`, follower 7; Chrome's own asking is
     still to be looked at: `gpu-priority-check asked`); (c) ~~the live
     lint and `tsession` desktops drawn in software, off the GPU
     altogether~~ done: a test session and its programs draw on the
     processors and hold no GPU device open (the whole live lint in
     32 s on dev builds so; HACKING, "Test desktops draw in
     software"), and a unit test never connects to a compositor; (d) ~~an agent's screen's recorder asks for a whole picture
     every second with nothing happening: from what changed instead
     (the viewer's `Painted`); a screen composited only when
     something looks~~ done, and with it what kept an idle agent's
     screen drawing (its Deskbar's widgets and clock, the keep-warm
     frame, statuses that changed without showing): 1.9% of a core
     and 90 wakes a second a screen to 0.1% and 8 (HACKING, "An
     agent's screen sits still"). **Left of it**: (d1) ~~a view that
     draws the same again still presents a frame~~ done
     (2026-11-21): the stage compares a drawing made again with the
     one it replaces whatever its size and whatever is in it, and
     the same is no damage (the charts example drawing the same
     twenty times a second: 200 frames in ten seconds to none, 8.6%
     of a processor to 0.9%; HACKING, "Only what shows, only what
     changed"); (d2) while an agent acts, the recorder
     takes the whole picture up to eight times a second through a
     file in the runtime folder (5 MB each at 1440 × 900, read back
     from the GPU): what changed only, from app_server's damage;
     (d3) an idle agent's screen holds 228 MB in nine programs
     (app_server 95, of it 71 its own; Tracker 37, Deskbar 31, the
     portal 26, notifications 25: measured 2026-11-20), ten screens
     2.3 GB on a computer that ran short. What app_server's was:
     **done** (2026-11-21). 37 MiB of it was the wallpaper thread's
     share of the heap, free and never given back (the C library
     raises its own thresholds once a large block has been freed, and
     `malloc_trim` leaves a thread's arena its end): the compositor
     holds the allocator to the thresholds it starts with
     (`olo_crash::give_memory_back`), 54.1 MiB of its own to 22.6 on a
     test desktop, at no cost in its time on the processors (HACKING,
     "Fast and light", Over time). **Left**: the same for the kit's
     apps cost a fifth more processor time in scrolling and typing
     (what a frame frees goes back and is faulted in again with every
     frame) and gained nothing at rest, so not yet: the thresholds
     tight while a window rests and loose while it draws (the kit
     knows which), or a frame's large blocks kept from frame to frame
     so that tight costs nothing, measured on an app that has shown
     pictures (Viewer after a photo, Tracker after a folder of them);
     the wallpaper's second copy in the compositor (its strips are on
     the GPU and in memory too, for a renderer that might ask again:
     5 MiB a screen at 1440 × 900, 59 at 5120 × 2880); what a first
     run's compiling of shaders leaves in Deskbar and Tracker (8 to
     16 MiB more than a later run's, Mesa's and in use: a cache
     warmed at install, or compiled out of the process); and the
     notification service and the portal started when first needed
     there; (e) the kit recovering from a lost device in
     place, not by starting again (blade's device made anew, the
     window's swapchain and caches rebuilt); (f) the driver's
     behaviour written up for its people (a low queue's wait is not
     a failed firmware), for Ben to send; (g) a kernel patch of
     Olo's for it, as for windows' buffers (`kernel/gpu-memory`), if
     another program's low queue can still bring a reset: with Astra
     at max, as Ben said.
  2. **The person's desktop was never first on the GPU.** Its
     compositor asks EGL for High and EGL answers High, but Intel's
     drivers give it only to a process with CAP_SYS_NICE; Mesa asks
     the kernel for ordinary instead and says nothing (seen from the
     kernel: 1 where 2 was asked; with the capability, 2). Beside six
     ordinary programs drawing, an ordinary probe's draws waited 49 ms
     at the 99th percentile (56 at the worst), a high one's 22 (24).
     **Done, as the owner's choice** (Ben, 2026-11-20, told what
     it gives and why Astra's review had it taken out: "yes add the
     CAP_SYS_NICE thing"): Olo's login hands a person's Olo session
     the capability where `/etc/olo/compositor-first.d/UID` is there
     (the administrator's grant for that account), the
     session passes it to the person's app_server alone
     (`olo_system::caps`; HACKING, "The desktop first on the GPU").
     **Checked since** (2026-11-21, Linux 7.3.4): the driver's own
     word is asked for and shown (app_server asks xe as it takes a
     GPU up, logs it, tells it with the GPU list; Doctor says "The
     desktop comes first on the GPU" only on it), and for a probe it
     is as the capability says: an ordinary process is answered 1 and
     Mesa asks 1 for it, one given the capability is answered 2, asks
     2 and is given it (`gpu-priority-check asked`, which now shows
     the driver's answer). The compositor keeps the capability
     (queues are made later too). The file for everyone that came
     first is offered for removal.
     **Still to check on the computer**: the person's own compositor's
     line in the log and in Doctor after its next start with this
     build; that its draws wait less beside others drawing (a measure
     on the compositor itself, not a probe); the hand-over across a
     compositor restart, an upgrade and a display plugged in; the
     login's four programs at mixed versions.
  3. **The kernel's own worker threads run at the ordinary priority
     in the path of every frame and every key.** A frame the
     (realtime) compositor hands to the GPU is passed on by a kernel
     worker (the DRM scheduler's, `kworker/u…`), and a byte through a
     terminal's pty by another (`flush_to_ldisc`). Measured on the
     person's compositor, 30 s at a load of 29: 17% of its jobs
     waited over 1 ms for that worker, 3.6% over 4 ms, the worst
     27.6 ms; at a load of 23, 1.3% and 2.9 ms. Typing in Terminal
     was laggy then, with Claude Code answering each key in 2 to 4 ms
     and the compositor late on no frame. And Terminal's own threads
     on that path (`termd reader`, `termd writer`, `shell output`)
     are at nice 0, with five of olo-termd's whose raise rtkit
     refused. **Done**: a kernel setting, **Short turns** (the
     scheduler's base slice at its base, 0.7 ms, where the kernel
     comes with 2.8 on this many processors: Preferences ▸
     Performance ▸ Kernel, Doctor's `kernel:short-turns`,
     `olo-doctor --kernel short-turns on`): beside fifteen more busy
     programs, the kernel's workers waited over a millisecond six
     times less often, Terminal's threads seven times (their worst
     29 ms to 4), the compositor's hand-overs 14.5 ms to 5.7 at the
     worst (kernel/TUNING.md). **Done too** (2026-11-21): Terminal's
     own three threads on the path at the shell's tier (`termd
     writer`, `termd reader`, each `shell output`: their waits a run
     a third of what they were beside two burners a processor, and a
     tenth as many twentieths of a second with over a millisecond of
     waiting; HACKING has the figures), and a raise rtkit refuses
     asked for again (`raise_self_patiently`), so none stays at 0.
     **To do**: what is still left
     of those waits after it, and whether that wants a latency-first
     scheduler again (Olo's own threads are realtime now) or a
     kernel patch (the workers that pass GPU jobs and pty bytes on
     above ordinary work: with Astra, as Ben said); the guest's wake
     figures taken again on a quiet computer (`kernel-check turns`).
  Also found: memory. 102 GB had been written to swap in three days
  with tens of GB free throughout, and programs were held 2.9
  million times while the kernel made room. **Tried and withdrawn**
  (Ben: "i want the swap to only get used when absolutely necessary
  … make it an option in olo performance -> kernel on by default"):
  a kernel setting, Swap used last (`vm.swappiness` 0 with the
  kernel's older reclaim), which passed in the guest and, put on on
  Ben's loaded computer, ran it short within minutes: NVIDIA's
  driver failed an allocation, then its card's suspend, and the card
  stopped answering ("did you just kill my nvidia gpu?? i was using
  it"; "just remove that particular swap setting it's obviously
  dangerous"). Removed from Olo and from that computer the same
  hour; kernel/TUNING.md, "Tried and withdrawn", has what was
  measured, what happened and why the guest didn't show it. What is
  to be done instead is the next two items. And **the
  holding is for huge pages**: every program held making room in a
  20 s trace was asking for 2 MB pages (the linker 1,267 times, with
  3,595 compactions taking 8.8 s between them, one 311 ms; Chrome
  37 compactions): Fedora has such programs reclaim and compact for
  themselves (`transparent_hugepage/defrag`: madvise). Measured
  both ways (2026-11-21, in the guest and with a real link on this
  computer, nothing of it changed; kernel/TUNING.md, "Huge pages when
  asked for"): the linker that asks is a seventh quicker for them and
  is the one that waits; deferring them is a trade, and isn't
  offered. **But the threads that draw were held for 2 MB pieces
  too, having asked for none: the GPU driver's memory pool asks on
  their behalf** (`sudo tools/dev/memory-holds`, new; ten minutes of
  the usual load: Chrome's GPU process held 591 times, the longest
  327 ms, a kit app's drawing thread 390 ms, a window's thread
  458 ms, the compositor's loop 7 ms; Linux 7.3 has the pool try
  hard for them; TUNING.md, "Graphics memory in 2 MB pieces").
  **Built** (2026-11-21, with Astra from the design on, as Ben said
  of anything in the kernel: a design review and four reviews of
  what was built, every must-fix taken; the last says yes to one
  trial on this build with its owner's word, and the offer stays
  held): `olo_gpu_pages`,
  a module whose probe has the pool's 2 MB try made without waiting
  for one device on xe; it checks itself as it loads before it
  touches anything real, and is loaded only into a kernel it was
  checked in (`kernel/gpu-pages/QUALIFIED`); its service names its
  load and touches no other; Olo Doctor's card and the Kernel tab's
  sixth box (Drawing) say what is so. **Not offered, and nothing
  switches it on** (`GRAPHICS_PAGES_OFFERED`): in guests it ends the
  holds, and no guest can say what it does to frames. **Waiting on
  Ben's word**: the trial on this computer, `sudo
  tools/dev/gpu-pages-try --on-this-computer` (twelve minutes, with a
  build looping and windows drawing beside it the same in every
  phase: on only while the tool holds the module's switch open, so
  whatever ends it puts the kernel back; itself tried in guests,
  stopped three ways). Then, before it is offered (TUNING.md has the
  review's list): the same runs repeated with frames, input and the
  GPU's work measured beside them and once with no tracing; the
  service around the driver's removal and the device's replacement;
  a real suspend, resume and reset; the guests' cases not yet
  covered. Still to do around it:
  - the write-up for the driver's people is drafted
    (docs/reports/ttm-pool-holds.md: a pool flag selected by xe,
    three lines; and xe's display page table made anew for every
    page flip, 180 a second on the compositor's loop), Ben's to

  - **every new kernel is out until a person has read it**
    (HACKING, "To qualify a kernel"). To do: the reading made
    quicker without being made less (the next kernel's ttm module

    `tools/dev/kernel-next` fetches it; the guests run on it), so an

  - kernels 6.19 to 7.2 wait at every size down to two pages, more

  - whether Olo's own programs make more GPU buffers than they

- **Background work is swapped first, and gives way on the processors
  and the disks as one group** (Ben, 2026-11-20, of swap: "how can we
  optimize what gets swapper better? i.e. can we somehow use the
  process priorities as an indication of how 'swappy' a certain
  process should be? so then the work that gets background priority,
  like rustc etc would be more likely to get swapped than interactive
  apps that will really impact me"; of the outline below: "yes
  perfect, implement it in full … however please also review your
  plan/design for it with astra 6.2 max to make sure it is sound and
  you haven't missed anything"). Linux has no link between a
  process's priority and reclaim, but reclaim is chosen by control
  group, and a group can be given protection (`memory.low`): the
  kernel takes from unprotected groups first and from a protected one
  only when nothing else is left. It orders, it doesn't forbid: swap
  stays whole (the rule the withdrawn setting left). On Ben's
  computer everything of the session is one group today
  (`session-N.scope`: 560 processes, 33 GB, the compositor and every
  agent's compiler together), so the kernel can't tell them apart.
  The outline: what the supervisor already lowers as background (its
  list of compilers, linkers and the like; a terminal's job busy for
  a minute) goes into a group of its own with no protection, an idle
  processor weight and a low disk weight; the desktop's group is
  protected. **The design was reviewed by Astra at max, and
  measured in the guest, and both changed it**
  (/var/tmp/claude-blueferry/groups/answer.md; guest runs in
  groups/guest/):
  - *Not `memory.low` on the desktop.* The review: Fedora's
    uresourced already owns the ancestors' budgets (it writes
    `MemoryLow=0` on user.slice and the user's slice at every change
    of who is at the computer), so a drop-in of Doctor's would be a
    second writer; and protection that covers memory which ought to
    be swapped has a cliff. The guest showed the cliff (1 GB, the
    multi-generational LRU, swappiness 1, a desktop group with an
    idle 200 MB program and a working set, a background group
    building): with the desktop protected for all it held, **the
    kernel ended a program (an OOM kill, with all of swap free)**
    where without groups nothing was ended. Splitting alone, with no
    protection, was no better than one group (the idle program was
    swapped out whole either way: 51,210 pages brought back). So
    nothing protects the desktop's memory from the kernel; nothing of
    Olo's may make an allocation fail that succeeds today.
  - *Instead the background group keeps to what is free*: its
    `memory.high` set by the supervisor, as memory fills, to what it
    holds plus what is free less a reserve. **Measured in the guest**
    (`kernel-check groups`, three guests each; kernel/TUNING.md,
    "Measured, to be built"): a desktop program in use waited a third
    as long at the 99th percentile (27 to 38 ms where 105 to 116)
    and a fifth as long at the worst; the system's services
    likewise; the build got a tenth fewer compiles done and little
    over half its files through; nothing ended, nothing refused. A
    program that sits idle for minutes is swapped all the same (its
    memory is the coldest there is, and swapping the build's own into
    compressed memory takes memory too): keeping it would mean
    stopping the build.
  - *Where the groups live*: inside the login session's scope
    (outside it a process loses its session, and under the user
    manager systemd-oomd watches and would end builds), made by Olo's
    login as root before the session starts: the root login worker
    parked in a leaf of its own that the account can't touch, a
    subtree handed to the account, the desktop and the background as
    leaves in it. A drop-in (`Delegate=`) so systemd leaves the
    subtree alone.
  - *Classified at birth*: a process moved later leaves what it
    already holds charged where it was. The build's driver (cargo,
    make, ninja…) is moved once, and every compiler it starts is
    born in the group; a test desktop puts itself there as it starts
    (`tsession`); an agent's screen is a third group, to be weighed.
  - ~~The supervisor's own fault found in review~~: a process
    lowered and then brought to the front is put back now (it stayed
    lowered until the supervisor was turned off). Its nice stays
    where it went: the account may not lower one (`RLIMIT_NICE` 0); a
    line in Doctor's limits file would let the supervisor put that
    back too, to be weighed.
  - *Processors*: the group idle against the desktop's (`cpu.idle`),
    measured on this computer with two scopes of the user manager
    before it is relied on; it does nothing for the kernel's own
    workers (they are outside every group), which is the Short turns
    setting's and a patch's. Disks: `io.weight` does nothing here
    (no I/O cost model, no BFQ on the NVMe queue), so the idle I/O
    class per thread stays.
  **Where it stands (2026-11-20, night): built the reviewed way, off
  as it comes.** A first build in the person's systemd manager was
  held on Astra's review (kernel/TUNING.md, "The first build, and why
  it was held"; kept on the local branch `background-group`). What is
  in now: Olo's login divides the session (`leader/`, `olo/desk`,
  `olo/bg` in the session's scope: `olo_system::session_groups`,
  tried against the kernel in a guest, 30 checks), the supervisor
  puts compilers and linkers in `bg` and one keeper holds it to its
  allowance (`olo_system::background`: a lock, read back at every
  look, a guard, the cache's credit by the desktop group's own
  waiting), Preferences has the choice ("Give compilers and linkers
  only spare memory", there only in a divided session), Doctor writes
  the drop-in that lets the login divide. Measured in guests with
  Olo's own keeper: a desktop program in use waited 6 and 16 ms at
  the 99th percentile where 90 and 92 as one group.
  **For Ben, to have it**: Olo Doctor's two fixes ("Olo's login
  screen runs an older version", "Builds can't be kept apart from
  the desktop"), then a restart or a new login; then the choice in
  Preferences ▸ Performance, which is theirs to turn on.
  **On Ben's computer, 2026-11-21, the first login with it**: the
  session is divided as built (`leader/` holding the login's worker,
  43 processes in `olo/desk`, `olo/bg` idle with no allowance, the
  four files Ben's, everything else root's), logind has the session
  active with its leader, and Ben turned the choice on. **Seen under
  a real load that night** (a release build of the workspace beside
  other agents' builds: fifteen compilers in `bg`, a load of 30 to 40,

  23% of five minutes and 10% of one, the desktop's group 0.07% and

  **Left**:
  - On Ben's computer: external apps still

- **The NVIDIA card can never again be left stuck and unrecoverable**
  (Ben, 2026-11-20: "can you also put an astra 6.2 max agent on
  trying to figure out at a low level how we can unfuck the nvidia
  card without rebooting / restarting everything"; "after upgrading
  olo doctor came up with this and now it's stuck on 'fixing'"; "how
  can we prevent the nvidia card from being stuck and unrecoverable
  again in the future?"; "can we create our own olo version of the
  nvidia driver that fixes this bug?"; of the five things below and
  the patched driver: "let's do the patch as well as 1 through 5 all
  of them make it all rock solid bulletproof").
  What happened: memory ran short (the withdrawn swap setting);
  NVIDIA's driver failed an allocation; a minute and a half later
  the card's runtime suspend failed (its last check, whether the
  firmware's processor had halted, was made against the driver's
  one deadline for the whole call, already three seconds past: "GSP
  unload failed at suspend"); the driver was left half suspended
  with no way back, the kernel's power management for the card in
  an error state. Then Doctor's own fix for that ("Start It Again",
  which had worked on 2026-11-07) unloaded NVIDIA's display module,
  and the kernel never came back from it (`nvEvoMakeRoom`: a wait
  with no end). The investigation (Astra at max, read against the
  driver's source 615.71.09 and Linux 7.2.15;
  /var/tmp/claude-blueferry/nvhelp/answer.md): no way out on that
  boot short of a restart, and no order of calls that would have
  been safe (HACKING, "A graphics card that stopped answering").
  **Done**: (2) Doctor says the state and offers nothing that can
  hang; a request for the old restart is refused before its first
  step. The stuck thread was put out of the way by hand (idle class,
  one slow core: 91% of a performance core to 6%). The write-up for
  NVIDIA is kernel/nvidia/report-615.71.09-runtime-suspend.md, for
  Ben to send.

  2. ~~Doctor never unloads a driver whose card doesn't answer~~;

  3. **Far fewer suspends.** The card suspended and woke 455 times

  4. **No suspend while memory is short: in the driver, not from
     outside.** Built as a hold from the follower (the card's

- **A title an agent sets lands on another window's tab** (Ben,
  2026-11-21: "terminal app is mixing up tab names"). **Done**, the
  cause: Codex's tool calls and hooks come from its app server, one
  daemon for every Codex window and a child of whichever came first,
  and the tab was found by the asker's process family before the
  folder it gave: every Codex session was taken to be in that first
  window's tab. An asker that comes through such a server is now found
  by the folder alone, and asked for one when it gives none
  (`agent_context::Asker`; HACKING, the tab titles). Shown headless
  both ways: `tools/dev/agent-title-check` fails on the build from
  before and passes now. **Left**: two sessions of the same agent in
  one folder still can't be told apart by the folder (the first tab
  running that agent is taken): the hook, which runs once at a
  session's start, could hand the agent a word for its tab to give
  back with each title, if Codex's hook is run where the session is;
  and the same for what the hook tells an agent about its tab's group.

- **The command key's Shift in a terminal** (found 2026-11-21, making
  Rex's keys). A terminal-style window (Terminal, Rex) gets ⌘X and ⇧⌘X
  as one chord: app_server adds a Shift to the command key's chords for
  every terminal, and the kit's `MenuBar::raw` looks for them so. In
  Terminal, of Undo and Redo, Find Again and Find Previous, whichever
  is on answers to both keys (⇧⌘Z undoes while only Undo is on; ⇧⌘G
  finds again). Rex avoids such pairs for now (⌥⌘D, ⌥⌘C, ⌥⌘G where
  ⇧⌘D, ⇧⌘C, ⇧⌘G belong). A first fix (Olo's own terminals sent the
  chords as pressed, told by the right Ctrl alone) worked in headless
  tests and was withdrawn on Astra's review; whatever replaces it has
  to hold all of these:
  - physical Ctrl held with ⌘ (Ctrl, then ⌘, then V) must not become
    the command (it pasted): both Control sides travel with each input,
    and a command-only shortcut is refused when the left one is down;
  - with no keyboard profile read (outside Olo, a first read failed)
    plain Ctrl+V must not match a command: a terminal keeps Ctrl+Shift
    keys then;
  - an old Terminal with a new app_server, or the reverse (the
    installer goes on after one binary fails), must not send ⌘C to the
    shell as an interrupt while Copy is on: the two sides have to agree
    (the app announces it, the server answers), not assume;
  - a held key's repeats after ⌘ is let go read as Control with the key
    (true today in Terminal: ⌘D then D held);
  - ⌘ with Page Up/Down, Ctrl+Shift+Home with Windows' keys and what
    an unbound ⇧⌘R sends a program that asked for kitty's key reports
    all change once Shift is real: decide each;
  - a text field in a terminal's window gets ⌘⌫ as Ctrl+U and does
    nothing with it (Find, in both apps).
  (Done meanwhile, 2026-11-23, for the kit's text widgets: the
  clipboard's keys, Select All and undoing work in every field of a
  terminal app, its dialogs too, by reading the Shift app_server adds
  as not the person's: `keys::own_shift`, HACKING. It is this item's
  cure that would let ⇧⌘Z redo there, and ⌘← and ⌘→ go to a line's
  ends in those fields: today they select by a word, the Shift
  counted.)
  The same review, of Rex's own handling, still open: its pane encoder
  drops modifiers on keys it doesn't know (BeOS's Alt+Left, ⌥⌘R, kitty
  reports); the configuration's keys are read for this computer's
  server only and a sequence begun in one window counts in another.

    key late, in Rex and in whatever else draws from the render state.
    The cure is that one line in the engine and the library built
    again (`tools/build-ghostty-vt.sh`, which wants to apply a patch

  - *The damage path at the edge of a float* (the kit; found by
    Astra's three reviews of the comparison in place, 2026-11-22, with
    reproductions through the painter, the stage and a frame's
    assembly; all of them in the code before that change too). Bounds
    are a corner and a size in f32, and what is skipped or cut by them
    is decided on `corner + size`: far from where a drawing began
    (millions of device pixels), or at fractions that aren't halves
    and quarters, a join or a cut can end a pixel short of what shows,
    and that column isn't drawn again in a frame of parts. Seen: a
    fold of `union`s (three glyphs at -6,000,000, 2 and -12,000,000:
    ends at 8, shows to 8.625); `intersect` (a quad from -16,777,216
    to 2 cut from -16,777,215: ends at 1); the stage moving a joined
    rectangle by its corner (`stage::damage`'s `place`: ends at 4, the
    quad at 5); damage and assembly adding an item's and a layer's
    offsets in different orders (+9,000,000 and -9,000,000: damage
    says [0, 1), the frame draws to 1.75); a path's bounds from
    `push_triangle`'s unions, and scaled corner and size apart
    (`Path::scale`: a right edge of 3.5 at 2.5× cached as 8, drawn to
    8.75); a line of glyphs whose corner is 33,554,432 away (the
    glyph's bearing lost taking it from the corner: drawn a pixel
    off). The cure Astra names: keep the four edges (a least and a
    most don't round) through grouping, the tests of what is over
    what, and clipping, and make a corner and a size only where one is
    needed; never pad (a pad is a frame for nothing: HACKING, "Fast
    and light"). (The one of them at ordinary coordinates is done: a
    sprite turned or moved by its matrix reaches its clip,
    `Primitive::reach`. Nothing of Olo's turns one: `paint_svg` has no
    caller.)

        against SSH; the rig needs a slow link for UDP (delay, loss,
        rate) for it.

        stream.

        carries the link; Rex's reconnection above it is to be tried).

        and why not.

  - *Files from a host, and folders kept in step* (Ben, 2026-11-22:
    "thinking about what we'll need to use rex to build olo (as an
    example), once it's built we'd want an easy way to e.g.
    download/sync the release artifacts locally. do you have ideas on
    how we could add this in a way that feels very intuitive and
    rex+olo native? i'd want a way to do it in the rex client myself …
    and also of course the coding agents should be able to do it
    themselves too with instructions in the skill or wherever they
    belong. and i wonder if we could go even further with the concept
    of maybe having specific dirs (optionally recursive) auto synced
    (with the ability to do it one way -- either way -- or 2-way) and
    obv. that would also be configurable/manageable by the coding
    agents and in the ux. it should all be really intuitive and
    ergonomic both for agents and humans. figure out the most intuitive
    way to do this -- also ask gemini 4 neon via agy it tends to have
    some good ideas on this kind of thing -- and add this feature").
    What another agent told Ben, which they passed on: the client
    crate already carries a file down in pieces
    (`terminal_download_begin`, `BytesDataStream`, over the one
    connection), so what is missing is the client's side: written to
    disk as it comes, not gathered in memory as Quick Look's is, with
    progress as an upload has; ways in (Quick Look, the path browser, a
    pane's menu; or asked for from the host, behind a permission of
    its own in Preferences ▸ Rex); and care with what can be run (the
    answer says nothing of a file's mode, and what came from a host
    isn't run without the person's say). To do, in this order: ask
    Gemini (`agy`) for ideas, with nothing private in the asking; set
    the design down (what a person does: drag out of a pane or a
    listing? a Downloads place? a folder "kept in step" shown where,
    with what marks; what an agent does: the `rex` command and the
    bridge's, said in the skill); then one file, a folder, and folders
    kept in step one way, the other, and both.
    And as little sent as can be (Ben, the same day: "when syncing
    files/folders it would be very important to do it as optimally as
    possible, minimizing data transfer where possible via compression,
    file deltas, whatever is possible (really we should get it as close
    to mathematically optimal as possible for the syncs)"): what is
    already on the other side isn't sent again (pieces known by their
    content, so a file moved, renamed or changed in part costs its
    changed pieces; a file the other side has under another name,
    nothing), what is sent is compressed, and what a sync cost is
    measured against what the change was (bytes on the wire for a
    build's artifacts changed by one file, by one byte, by nothing).
    **The design** (2026-11-24; Gemini's proposal, kept at
    `/var/tmp/claude-olo/rex-sync/gemini-design.md` while this is
    built, weighed and cut down here): one engine, `crates/rex-sync`, a
    library both ends link (the app, and the helper Olo already puts on
    each host, `olo-rex-link sync`, spoken over `exec_io` first and a
    QUIC stream of the link later). What one side has is an index (each
    file's size, time, mode, BLAKE3, and its content-defined chunks, the
    gear hash diskbackup's chunker uses, 4/16/64 KiB, each known by 128
    bits of BLAKE3), kept so a look at an unchanged tree reads nothing;
    the receiver says what it has, the sender sends per file the
    cheapest recipe: nothing (the same), a copy of what the receiver
    holds under any name (moves, copies: no bytes), the old file's
    prefix and the new tail (a file that only grew: an agent's
    transcript, a log), the chunks the receiver lacks, compressed with
    zstd (the old bytes around as its prefix where that helps; small
    files batched in one stream; what doesn't compress sent raw); the
    receiver builds each file beside its place and checks its whole
    BLAKE3 before renaming it in. A host never names a path of this
    computer's: what a host sends lands in a folder of the person's
    choosing per host (Downloads ▸ Rex ▸ HOST unless said), and a kept
    folder only where the person made it, with a permission of its own
    in Preferences ▸ Rex. In this order, each useful alone: (1) the
    engine and Agent Sessions' copy through it (only what changed, the
    item below); (2) one file or folder down or up, from a pane's path
    menu, Hosts, and agents (`olo pull`, `olo send`); (3) folders kept
    in step one way (watchers both ends: inotify, the helper's), Rex's
    Synced Folders window; (4) agents' control (`olo sync …`); (5) both
    ways, with conflicts kept as copies, never lost; (6) Tracker's and
    Deskbar's marks. Measured at each step against the change: bytes on
    the wire for a 200 MB transcript and 4 KiB appended, a binary with
    one function changed, a tree of 50,000 files with one edited, a
    rename, nothing changed; and idle costs nothing.
    *The engine* is built (2026-11-24, HACKING, Rex, "Files kept in
    step: the engine"): 60 B for nothing changed in 5,000 files, 713 B
    for 4 KiB appended to 200 MB (written in place there), 7.1 KiB for
    a byte changed in 50 MB, 380 B for a rename. And the helper's side,
    `olo-rex-link sync` (HACKING, "A helper on the host"), driven by the
    app over SSH (`olo_rex_client::sync`). And Agent Sessions' copy
    through it (HACKING, Rex, "The agents' sessions": a scoped receiver
    looking at the copied files alone, what each was made into kept
    here): a turn added to a 30 MB transcript sends its line, 566 bytes
    (the archive sent the whole, 438 KB compressed, at each change).
    And step (2) for agents: `olo send PATH…` on a host saves files and
    folders here in Downloads ▸ Rex ▸ HOST, under a permission of its
    own (HACKING, the bridge, "Files a host sends"); a rebuilt archive
    sent again sends its change. The person's way in is Tracker's (the
    item "A host's folders in Tracker"). And step (3) from a host:
    `olo sync PATH` keeps a host's folder in step here, brought again
    moments after it changes there (the helper's watch, no polling), with
    `ls`, `wait`, `stop` (HACKING, the bridge, "Folders kept in step").
    Next: the Host window's list of them (in its tabs), one kept the
    other way (here to a host), the person's own way in, then both ways.

- **SSH sessions that don't stall under load; Terminal and Rex first in
  line** (Ben, 2026-11-22: "look into whether there's a way to prioritize
  ssh sessions and traffic on olo desktop, like maybe under prefs ->
  performance a way to put ssh sessions on rtkit or give them super high
  priority or something and also if possible prioritize their network
  traffic. basically under load (whether machine/cpu or network) i don't
  want ssh sessions stalling. and it should also include making sure olo
  terminal and rex has real time priority too (but not all the processes
  they launch, only the gui app itself and the terminal sessions)").
  After the Rex work. To find out first: what an `ssh` (and Rex's own
  in-process SSH, and `sshd` for sessions coming in) waits on when the
  machine is loaded (the processor: its scheduling class and cgroup
  weight; the network: its packets' class, DSCP and the queue on the
  way out), measured (keys to echo over SSH with the processors and the
  link each saturated, before and after). Then the least that cures it:
  a real-time or raised priority for the terminal's own threads (the
  window and the pty's reader and writer, not the shell and what it
  runs: those must stay as they are, and must not inherit it), through
  rtkit or the session's own grant, as the window server has; the
  network side (a socket's priority and its packets' marking, a queue
  that serves them first); and a switch under Preferences ▸
  Performance saying what it does. Nothing that starves the rest: a
  limit on what the raised threads may take.
  Done 2026-11-24 (HACKING, the tiers): the processor's side, measured
  (a key to its echo over SSH beside 64 nice-0 burners on 32
  processors: worst 13.7 ms, 5.2 raised; the middle 0.1 ms either way:
  the kernel's scheduler wakes a key's few microseconds of work first
  as it is): Terminal's and Rex's windows' threads and Rex's I/O threads
  at the shell's tier (−5), and an `ssh` reading a terminal raised there
  by the supervisor (one reading a pipe left as work). Found: OpenSSH's
  `ObscureKeystrokeTiming` (on since 9.5) holds every key to a 20 ms
  beat, whatever the load (middle 19 ms at rest): a privacy feature;
  whether to offer to turn it off for the person's hosts is theirs to
  say. Left: the network's side (each packet's class, a queue on the way
  out that serves a key's first: to be measured on a saturated link, as
  the Kernel tab's BBR was), and whether a switch under Preferences ▸
  Performance is wanted for what is now always on.

  attached files listed, saved and added, synced both ways; a key made

- **Token Pool: what its handover and claims still leave to chance**
  (2026-11-20; from Astra's reviews of the sign-in work above, checked
  against the code: each is how the pool works today, and each wants
  the design that work is parked for). In order of what it could cost:
  - *An unanswered claim is a field of its account's row.* Kept apart
    in the sealed store instead (provider, the provider's own name for
    the account, the grant or "the provider's choice", the request id,
    whether it was sent), it would outlive the row and a sign-in as
    another account: a late answer settles it, a return to the same
    account asks again by the same id, and one that can't be settled is
    shown, with a way to let it go by hand, while serving goes on.
  - *A renewal in flight at the instant of a handover* isn't under the
    store's lock (it began alone), and the new copy may renew the same
    account with the same rotating token: one of the two is refused,
    which signs the account out. A renewal should hold the handover
    off from before its request until it's kept (as claims do:
    `claims_closed`).
  - *The old copy's last renewal.* The new copy knows the old one has
    finished by its pipe closing, and from then saves without reading
    the file first: a renewal the old one wrote as it ended is written
    over by the new copy's next save, with the older sign-in. A last
    merge under the store's lock wants an order it doesn't have yet
    (tried on the branch, 2026-11-20, and taken out: run before the
    vault was open it wrote an empty store): the store shared until that merge is
    done, whichever of a save, a renewal or the pipe's reader sees the
    end first; and a save that takes in other accounts' renewals
    without taking back the one just made (by which was renewed here,
    not by expiry).
  - *A re-sign-in during a claim's network round trip* is treated as
    one just after it (the result is guarded, the spend isn't): a
    guard shared by the send and by replacement and removal would make
    the two take turns.
  - *Late records* (`Late`, over the handover's pipe): one that
    arrives before the vault is open is booked against an empty pool
    and lost; a limit seen by the old copy is dated when
    its answer came, not when its request went, so one sent before a
    reset here and answered after it puts the account back at its
    limit until the next read. Kept until the vault opens; a reset
    epoch on what's sent, shared across the handover.

- **kache: clean-up that isn't starved by a command left running**
  (2026-11-21, from Ben's "check whether there are old debug builds or
  anything that can be cleaned up" and "make it so old builds we no
  longer need will get cleaned up automatically"; AGENT-NOTES, "Old
  builds", and kache's FORK.md have what was found). Every clean-up
  step of kache's takes one lock for the whole computer, which every
  Cargo command holds for as long as it runs: with another project's
  `cargo watch` commands running from login to logout, nothing is
  cleaned but around a restart. **Done**: units unused for three days
  go where thirty were kept; an ended Codex agent's builds removed
  after a day; holder records from before a restart dropped;
  `tools/dev/prune-graphs`, which reclaims idle incremental graphs
  under kache's own lock at a moment when it is free (1,230 graphs,
  131 GB of 158, were taken once by its first form). **Tried and
  taken out, each on Astra's reproduction with real Cargo**: in the
  fork, clean-up going ahead when every holder works in another
  workspace (a `cargo test` lost its test binary between building and
  running it; a configured target directory, `cargo -C`, an alias, a
  symlink all point where the inference doesn't look), and the graph
  sweep sharing the lock (`cargo clean` shares it too and replaces
  the folder under held locks: a later build's graph deleted under
  that build's own lock); here, the first form of `prune-graphs`,
  which went by Cargo's and the units' locks through folder
  descriptors (an interrupted `cargo clean` leaves the unit's folder
  with a new lock and graph in it). **Left**:
  - What makes it happen by itself on this computer: the commands
    that hold the lock all day are `cargo watch`, which only starts
    other Cargo commands (each of which takes the lock for itself). A
    setting of the owner's in the fork that names such a command as
    holding no lock of its own ("this one only supervises"), off as
    it comes, reviewed by Astra as the rest was before it is
    installed; then kache's own clean-up finds its quiet minutes.
  - The sound general version in the fork (FORK.md says what it
    needs: leases that name the output roots a command will use, kept
    outside the trees clean-up renames; the graph sweep letting
    Cargo's locks go between units), designed and reviewed with Astra
    before a line of it is written.
  - Build folders kache doesn't know: a Codex agent's (its sandbox?),
    and one its registry forgot, which no later pass finds again
    though Git lists the worktree.

- **Translations as resources, not compiled in: measure it**
  (2026-11-19, from another agent's study of kache's misses, which Ben
  passed on: "packaging catalogs as separately updatable resources is
  worth measuring"; then: "Misses consumed 53.0 compiler-hours.
  Dependency changes accounted for 47.1 hours. In the main Olo checkout
  alone, 4,148 misses had identical source, flags, and every other
  recorded input except dependency artifacts … Start with translations
  … 22 commits touched them during this window. In six, the catalogs
  were the only shared-crate change. Shipping catalogs as versioned data
  would let a wording edit bypass recompilation of dependent apps. A
  one-string edit is a good benchmark"). The catalogs are compiled into
  olo-kit-base (`crates/kit-base/src/words.rs`), so every word added
  rebuilds the 41 apps built on it, and the pre-push hook builds the
  whole workspace in release (`tools/hooks/pre-push`). Read at start
  instead, as versioned data (from the build's or the installed share
  folder), a catalog change would rebuild nothing. Measure first, with a
  one-string edit: the builds it costs now and after, against a read at
  each app's start (and what in-place reload, tests and agents' screens
  need); then do it if it pays.
  **Measured, and done** (2026-11-20; HACKING, "Words in the person's
  language", "The catalogs are data, read at start"). A one-word edit
  of the German catalog, release, this computer: 48 crates built again,
  2 min 35 s for the workspace; and 38 of the 81 programs each carried
  all twelve catalogs (3.5 MB). Against a read at start: 0.2 ms for a
  program starting in a language other than English (268 KB read, then
  the same 1 ms making its table), nothing in English. It pays, so the
  catalogs are data now: `data/words/CODE.txt`, read by each program
  the first time a word is wanted, installed with the other data and
  brought along by each upgrade; the same edit builds nothing (0
  crates, 0.7 s). Tests, the lints and test sessions read the tree's.
  To know: a change of words alone, like a change of icons alone,
  isn't offered as an upgrade (nothing was built): it comes with the
  next one. And the first upgrade onto this is made by a session that
  doesn't know to bring the catalogs: programs read the tree's until
  the upgrade after it does.

- **An agent screen asks for a password it hasn't been given** (Ben,
  2026-11-24: "agent screens needs to support a way for an agent to
  request access to a credential not yet shared with them. it should
  show the permissions prompt on the user's desktop and auto approve if
  auto approve is on. this also means that olo passwords should show all
  available items shared or not but only the non-secret fields are
  available when not shared and they will need to request access to get
  the secrets if not shared. and make it easy for them to use like have
  the extension still offer to fill password etc but then it
  automatically requests the unshared secret"). Today a screen's
  Passwords holds only what the person shared with it (HACKING,
  "Passwords for agent screens": a sealed copy of those items), so an
  agent can't see what else there is, nor ask. Wanted:
  - The screen's copy holds every item, those not shared with it as
    their non-secret fields alone (title, username, website, vault,
    kind, tags: what Screen ▸ Passwords for Every Screen… already lists),
    marked so in its list ("Not shared: ask for it"); a secret of one is
    never in the copy.
  - Asking, three ways, one request: Request Access in the screen's
    Passwords (the item's details); `op read`/`op item get --reveal` of
    one on the screen (waits for the answer, saying it asked the person
    on the desktop); and the extension's fill: an unshared login is
    offered for the page as a shared one is, and choosing it asks, then
    fills once allowed (a passkey the same).
  - The question on the person's desktop, never on the screen, from
    their own Passwords (over the keychain socket, which knows the
    asker is on a screen: `shared::on_a_screen`): "Allow the agent on
    “SCREEN” to use “GitHub”?", which field, for which site, with Deny
    (the default), Allow Once (the secret handed for this one use, not
    written into the screen's copy) and Share With This Screen (added
    to its shares, as the Passwords tab would). Asked while Passwords is
    locked: it asks to be unlocked first, as `op` does. Under the tray's
    Approve Without Asking: allowed at once (once, not shared), said in
    a quiet notification, as Passwords says op's changes.
  - Each ask and its answer in the screen's history (`actions.jsonl`,
    as passkeys' uses are) and in `olo-screen history`; the skill for
    agents says how to ask and that the person may say no.
  - Tried headless: the copy's unshared items without a secret, each
    way of asking (allowed, denied, under Approve Without Asking,
    Passwords locked), the extension's fill after the answer.

- **A passkey shared with an agent screen wasn't offered there** (Ben,
  2026-11-18, the google-setup screen: "google showed its own qr code
  thing for a passkey instead -- the olo passwords extension didn't
  inject its own one and offer it up"). **Found and fixed** (the second
  investigator found it; HACKING.md, "The keychain"): Google's request
  did reach Olo's extension, but the screen's Passwords served nothing.
  It had been quit and opened again while the first still ran on for
  what it had copied, holding the keychain and SSH-agent sockets; the
  new one found them "already served", and once the old one went,
  nothing answered ("Passwords isn't running"), so Chrome showed its own
  QR sheet. A quitting Passwords now lets go of its sockets first. Made
  to happen and stop happening in a test session. Try: once upgraded,
  a sign-in with a shared passkey on a screen. (Whether Google's
  request names the shared passkey's credential is still to see: with
  nothing answering, it was never asked.)

- **Agent Screens: every action says what the screen looks like after
  it** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "can you improve olo agent screens reliability
  by having it always include a new / up to date screenshot of the
  screen after each command is run (as well as the widget tree and
  whatever else we already give it)? i want the agent to always know
  what the latest state is"). Each `olo-screen` action (click, set,
  select, key, type, scroll, wheel, drag, invoke, the window commands,
  run) waits for the screen to settle (as `wait --idle` does), takes a
  picture of it, and gives its path in the action's JSON beside the
  focused window's widget tree as it is then (today an action says
  only what it matched and what has the focus), so an agent never acts
  on what it last saw. What it costs an action measured (the picture's
  and the settling's milliseconds), and a way to leave it out for a
  run of quick actions. **Done** (HACKING.md, "Every action says how
  the screen is after it"): every action's `after` is read once the
  screen has stopped changing for a quarter of a second and no page is
  loading (the extension now says when a tab is, so a link's click
  answers with the new page), with a `picture` of the screen, the
  focused window's `tree` and the `windows`; ~305 ms an action against
  76 quick (`--quick`, `OLO_SCREEN_QUICK=1`). Also found: each screen's
  recorder left a 5 MB frame in memory once its screen stopped (31 MB
  of six stopped screens'), and `look` piled its pictures up in memory:
  both on disk or removed now. Try: any agent's next actions on a
  screen, once upgraded (Chrome takes the extension's 1.15.6 as it
  next starts).

- **Desktop icons gone after Deskbar is collapsed and expanded** (Ben,
  2026-11-18: "i tried the new collapse deskbar then expand again. it
  worked but the desktop icons all disappeared and didn't come back").
  **Found and fixed**: neither Deskbar nor Tracker, but app_server out
  of file descriptors (696 open of a limit of 1,024; the fold made
  every window draw anew): the kernel dropped what Terminal and
  Tracker sent and both were disconnected, 13:16:26. Every Olo program
  raises its limit as it starts now, and Olo Doctor raises it for
  those running (HACKING.md, "Open files"). **Still to find**: why
  Tracker, unlike Terminal, didn't re-execute and reconnect when its
  connection went: **found and fixed** too (a loop ended in an error
  was asked whether its socket had hung up yet; HACKING.md, "What a
  day's logs showed").

- **The pointer vanishes over a video in Chrome and Chrome-based apps**
  (Ben, 2026-11-18: "sometimes when a cursor goes over a video on
  chrome or a chrome based app like slack then the cursor doesn't show
  again until i move the mouse completely out of the window and back.
  the cursor shouldn't disappear when over a video at all, it should
  only ever disappear if in full screen and hasn't moved for 5s and then
  come back if it moves again"). Tried before, still there.
  **Done so far**: Olo holds that rule itself now (`pointer_hide`,
  HACKING.md "A program hiding the pointer"), so a rested pointer comes
  back on the first move whatever the program does. **The cause, found
  and fixed** (by the Codex helper, `olo-debug-help`, checked and
  applied): olo-wlproxy couldn't make Chrome's cursor-shape device
  again after app_server restarted, and dropped every shape from then
  on (HACKING.md, the proxy's "An object is made again…";
  `tools/dev/cursor-replay-check`). A Chrome or Slack already running
  gets the mended proxy when it's next started.

- **A Calendar app, native, with Google and Fastmail calendars** (Ben,
  2026-11-17: "build a beautiful olo native calendar app. add calendar
  support to prefs -> integrations and support any number of google
  calendars (eg from multiple google accounts) as well as any number of
  fastmail calendars. make sure it is full features, integrates with all
  the olo stuff, looks beautiful. it should be able to aggregate all the
  connected calendar sources into one unified calendar view, and also
  support read and write actions"). `olo-calendar`: day, week, month and
  agenda views of every connected calendar together, each in its colour,
  shown or hidden; events made, changed, moved and deleted, repeating
  ones and invitations too, written back to where they live.
  Preferences ▸ Integrations ▸ Calendars: any number of Google accounts
  (Google Calendar's API, signed in as Drive is) and of Fastmail ones
  (CalDAV, or JMAP for Calendars, with an app password kept in
  Passwords). Olo's own: reminders as notifications, a Deskbar widget
  (what's next), the clock's menu, the command palette, the phone, an
  agents' API, in-place reload, native in Rust. **So far**
  (2026-11-18): the engine's first parts, `crates/calendar`
  (`olo-calendar`): iCalendar read and written back whole (`ical`),
  repeating worked out (`rrule`: the RFC's examples are its tests), and
  events with their zones, exceptions and occurrences (`event`).
  Then CalDAV for every account (`dav`), the accounts and their
  sign-ins (`account`: Google's by OAuth with the person's own client,
  as Drive; Fastmail's by app password), calendars kept on disk in step
  with their servers (`store`) and a stand-in server to test with
  (HACKING.md, "Calendar's engine"). Then the app itself
  (apps/calendar, `olo-calendar`; HACKING.md, "Calendar"): the small
  month and the calendars at the left, Day, Week, Month and Agenda,
  every calendar in its colour, kept in step with its servers; and
  events made, changed and deleted (the event's window; "only this
  one" or all of a repeating event; never over a change made somewhere
  else), by the menus, a double-click or the keyboard. And accounts
  added in Preferences ▸ Integrations ▸ Calendars: Google's by signing
  in (the client DiskBackup's Drive set-up made is found, the CalDAV
  API to be turned on in its project), Fastmail's by an app password,
  any other CalDAV server's; tried against a stand-in server end to
  end. Its own icon (a block calendar, in every set; Flat's its own
  drawing). An event is dragged among the hours to another time or
  day (HACKING.md, "Calendar"). Undo and Redo of every change (a
  deletion asks nothing now). Find (⌘F: every calendar shown, from a
  year back to two years on, listed by day from today). An event's
  end is dragged by its bottom edge (how long it lasts), and events
  are dragged among the month's days and the whole-day strip.
  Invitations: how each looks says what you answered, Edit ▸ Reply and
  the event window's Going answer them, and the window lists the
  guests with their answers; the Invite field invites people to an
  event of your own (the server sends the invitations).
  Deskbar widgets: Next Event and The Day Ahead (Preferences ▸
  Deskbar; a click opens Calendar on the event). The command palette
  finds events (Return opens Calendar on one). An assistant (View ▸
  Show Assistant: questions answered from your events, with links to
  them, and events drafted for you to save; Preferences ▸ AI ▸
  Calendar). The clock's menu (a click on Deskbar's date and time: the
  day, what's still to come today and tomorrow, Open Calendar, Date &
  Time Settings…). The phone: its calendar's reminder of an event
  Calendar reminds of here isn't shown twice (not tried with a phone).
  Reminders are shown
  (`olo-calendar --service`, a session service; Show goes to the
  event). (Its cost
  is measured and in-place reload tried: HACKING.md, "Calendar".)
  **Not tried against Google's and Fastmail's real servers**: that
  needs Ben's accounts. **For Ben, to try**: Preferences ▸ Integrations
  ▸ Calendars ▸ Add an Account… (for Google, first turn on the CalDAV
  API in the Google Cloud project of DiskBackup's client: the link is
  in the form; for Fastmail, an app password with access to calendars),
  then open Calendar.

- **Notifications, made plain: one model for what shows, stays, fades
  and is read** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "the red vs blue types and what fades
  out vs goes to history/archive vs goes away vs automatically gets
  marked as read vs what doesn't etc. is all very confusing. can you
  spin up an opus 5.5 agent on xhigh and ask it to do a thorough visual
  analysis of notifications and all the different edge cases, the
  notifications app and how they appear in the deskbar and on window
  title bars and how they transition etc. etc. and then ask it to
  research what the best practices are around notifications and alerts
  for web apps, other desktop environments, phones etc. and have it
  give you specific suggestions/guidance on how we can revamp olo
  notifications to be more intuitive"). *The study is done* (an Opus
  5.5 agent at xhigh, as asked: the one time the no-subagents rule is
  set aside, by Ben's word; 2026-11-18): its report, with a matrix of
  every edge case, pictures of each state, sources, and a proposed
  model, is at `/var/tmp/opus-notif/report.md` (pictures in
  `/var/tmp/opus-notif/shots/`). What it found, in short: two different
  things are drawn with the same marks (a notification, and an app's
  own "waiting" count made into a fake list item that turns the app's
  real notifications red); red means four things and × means four
  things; unread notifications leave by a timer and land in the archive
  marked read; one an app withdraws stays unread and counted. *The
  model it proposes:* a notification is New (blue, counted on the bell,
  in blue), Read (no dot, fades with age, tidied away after a while) or
  Cleared (today's archive, each row saying when and why it left);
  Waiting (red) is only an app's own count, on its Deskbar row and
  tabs and in a "Waiting in apps" strip, never an item of the list and
  never recolouring notifications; urgency (Quiet, Normal, Urgent) is
  how one arrives, not a colour or a stop sign. Three rules: nothing
  New goes by itself; × always clears (with Undo); red is only waiting,
  blue only new. *Done, all twelve* (2026-11-18; HACKING.md, "The model, in one
  place"; four commits): the Cleared list saying why each left,
  waiting counts out of the list, urgency apart from "error", read on
  arrival in the app in front, counts and staying banners kept across
  restarts, one word and one count, what agents read, the small bugs.
  One thing decided against the study: a window's or tab's red dot
  still fades once you're there (it says where, not how much). **For
  Ben, to try** after an Upgrade: the bell's count is blue and counts
  only notifications; nothing unread disappears; × clears everywhere;
  View ▸ Cleared says why each left; an app's own count is under
  "Waiting in apps" and a red Inbox card with Later. *The list, in its order
  of benefit, each claim checked against the code first:* (1) unread never fades out
  (`History::fade_out`); (2) × clears on a banner too; (3) a withdrawal
  clears ("withdrawn by APP"); (4) waiting counts out of the list
  (`attention` items, `mark_waiting`, `more()` go; the strip and the
  Inbox's app cards come); (5) the bell counts New, in blue; (6)
  urgency apart from kind (a call is urgent, not an error); (7) read
  on arrival in the app in front, without the dwell's race; (8) red
  counts, sticky banners and actions kept across restarts and
  upgrades; (9) one word and one count everywhere; (10) window and tab
  red dots follow what waits; (11) agents read state, urgency and why;
  (12) the small bugs it met (a read row among the unread, a duplicate
  id after a replacement, the cube icon on banners, "+N more" for
  queued banners). *Decided as built* (Ben, the same day: "for the
  notifications stuff i want you to decide and use your judgement --
  overall i think the findings were spot on, you should use your
  taste/judgement for any decisions and if needed consult opus 5.5
  xhigh for a second opinion"; the report's recommendations are where
  each starts): where the red counts live (a strip
  and app cards); what the bell counts and its colour (New, blue);
  what a banner's × does (clears); what a withdrawn note becomes
  (cleared); whether the blue dot drains (yes, to a floor); how long
  before read ones are tidied (an hour); a note from the app in front
  (no banner unless urgent, read at once); tab dots (stay until dealt
  with); the names (Cleared; New or Unread, one of them).

- **A link opens in the Chrome window that's there, not a new one**
  (Ben, 2026-11-18, of a link clicked in Terminal: "it's not opening in
  my existing single chrome window it is opening a new chrome window.
  if there is one existing chrome window it should always open in that,
  and if more than one it should show the picker"). Chrome has four
  profiles here; a running Chrome opens a handed-over link in the
  profile it used last, and makes a window for it when that profile has
  none (its window was closed): reproduced in a test session (a second
  profile's window opened, used, closed; a link: a new window). With
  one window, Olo now has the window's own profile open the link (its
  extension, asked through its own host) and brings the window forward;
  the picker reaches the right profile too, where it reached whichever
  profile's host had started last. **For Ben**: after the next upgrade,
  Chrome takes the new extension (1.15.3) when it's next started; until
  then links open as before.

- **Olo Doctor's "still running an older version", after an upgrade**
  (Ben, 2026-11-18, of "sudo (1567566), olo-screen (2156913) … each runs
  a program file an upgrade has since replaced. Quit Them": "is that
  because they didn't upgrade properly or they are just in a graceful
  handover type state and should be left alone? i want to make sure that
  (a) we don't have an upgrade bug, and (b) it's not offering to
  terminate legit processes that should continue post upgrade"). Both
  were so. (b) `sudo` was olo-sudo running a script an agent had started
  from its shell hours before: a command, which ends by itself and which
  nothing would start again. olo-session knew to leave such a process
  (started by another program: "left alone (started by bash…)" in its
  log); Olo Doctor didn't have the rule, and offered to quit it. Now the
  rule is one function both go by (`olo_system::procs::
  started_by_another`), and Doctor says such commands among what's fine,
  with who started each. (a) The five `olo-screen` were each a running
  Agent Screen's frame recorder (`olo-screen record NAME`, which keeps
  the screen's history of frames): it ignored the upgrade's signal, so
  the session stopped it 90 s after as "still the old version", and
  nothing starts a running screen's recorder again: after any upgrade,
  running screens' frames were no longer kept. Now the recorder becomes
  the new version in place between two frames (the same process, a new
  segment), and a running screen with no recorder is given one at the
  agent's next action on it (one a screen, by a lock it holds). Tried
  on a screen of the agent's own in a runtime folder apart: replaced
  and signalled, it was the new version a second later and went on
  recording; stopped by hand, two actions at once started exactly one;
  it ended with its screen. **For Ben**: after the next upgrade, the
  screens running now (cx-1 … cx-5, qa-nocrm) get their recorders back
  at their agents' next action; their frames between 11:39 today and
  then weren't kept. Doctor's finding goes once this build is installed
  (the script it named is the agent's watch for the build-units item
  above, still running on purpose).

- **The embedded controller's event storm: Olo says so, and can keep
  the keys working** (Ben, 2026-11-17, of the two hours his brightness
  keys were dead and the laptop ran down on its charger: "i don't just
  want to restart i want this root caused"; "works now. so let's do two
  things: 1. add something to olo's supervisor to do this if an
  unsustainable backlog builds up, and 2. root cause and fix whatever
  happened here. there must be a bug somewhere"). What happened is in
  docs/AGENT-NOTES.md ("The embedded controller's event storm"). Done:
  the power follower no longer sets its plan at every flap; the
  supervisor watches for a storm and says so within seconds (a
  notification that stays, a Critical finding in Olo Doctor); and the
  guard is written as one of Olo's kernel modules (`olo_ec_storm`,
  HACKING, "The guard"): a handler in front of each of the firmware's,
  through the driver's own interface, so a flood of one event can't
  hold up the others. Olo Doctor suggests it ("Guard the Keys").
  **Waiting for Ben**: (1) installing the guard is yours to do, from
  Olo Doctor: it is checked as far as it can be without a controller
  that floods (its counting, its build, its refusal in a guest), and
  **has not run against your controller's real events**; after
  installing, the brightness keys, the lid and plugging the charger in
  and out are the things to try, and
  `cat /sys/module/olo_ec_storm/parameters/stats` says what it did.
  (2) The test of firmware 1.17: the same hand-over that failed
  (display unplugged, charger in, while running). (3) The reports, to
  the kernel's ACPI list (the EC driver queues query handlers without
  bound) and to Lenovo (the P1 Gen 9's controller reporting its adapter
  23 times a second): drafted in docs/reports/ec-query-backlog.md,
  yours to send or not.

- **AirPods' microphone with voice processing, named so in apps** (Ben,
  2026-11-18, of Teams in Chrome: "it still doesn't show the airpods
  device as 'Airpods (Voice Processing)' to tell me which one has the
  voice processing enabled"). What was wrong: your choice in
  Preferences ▸ Sound, "With AirPods: AirPods (Call Quality)", was
  kept and never acted on, so the computer's microphones went on being
  recorded from, and the processed microphone was (rightly) named for
  them. The AirPods service now makes the microphone you chose the
  input, as a pair connects and at once when the choice is changed;
  the processed microphone follows it and is named for it ("AirPods …
  (Voice Processing)"). Decided in code and tested there; **not tried
  with your AirPods** (you were on a call, and Olo's tests never
  connect a device). **To know before upgrading**: with that choice
  still set, the next time your AirPods connect (or the service starts
  with them connected) the input becomes their headset microphone, and
  their sound drops to call quality while something records. "AirPods
  (High Quality)" keeps music quality and uses their own microphone
  stream. **To try**: after an upgrade, look at the microphone list in
  Teams with AirPods in.

  Notifications, follow the link at the bottom right.

- **The built-in display's brightness, in HDR** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "the
  brightness settings on my builtin monitor are broken i can't turn
  them up or down"; "it's like i change it and then it just goes back
  to what it was"). Found: your panel is in HDR, where its backlight
  does nothing, and three things each put a brightness back (HACKING,
  "A display's brightness in HDR is SDR's white"): Preferences ▸
  Display's Brightness slider (and the IPC) moved the backlight while
  the keys moved SDR's white; the slider wasn't told the display's new
  level, so it went back to the old one after 0.6 s; and Preferences'
  older copy of the settings, given back with any other setting
  changed, undid what the keys had done. Now a display's brightness in
  HDR is SDR's white everywhere (keys, slider, agents), every change is
  told, and it is never taken from a client's copy.
  `tools/dev/brightness-check` reproduces it headless: 11 failures on
  the build you were running, none now. **To try**, after the upgrade:
  the brightness keys and Preferences ▸ Display's Brightness slider
  both move the built-in display's brightness in HDR and stay where
  they're put, with Preferences open or not; the bottom is still off.
  (Until you upgrade: the keys work while Preferences is closed, and
  "Everything else's brightness" under HDR in Preferences ▸ Display is
  the slider that works.)

- **Kernel settings that are a win for a desktop, a Kernel tab, and all
  of it kept across kernel updates** (Ben, 2026-11-16: "research what
  other linux kernel patches are recommended for high performance,
  responsive desktop operating systems and if you find any that are
  win-win over the fedora 45 kernel and would be a win for olo users then
  also integrate them into olo like bbr3 so that olo doctor can offer
  them. let's also have a new tab in the performance prefs for kernel
  tuning where this stuff can live and be configured and show any
  stats/details/data in there about the running patches too"; and "make
  sure all these kernel tunings/mods will continue to work properly
  after doing os updates that update the kernel"). *Done 2026-11-16.*
  kernel/TUNING.md is the account. Nearly all the desktop kernels carry
  is in Fedora 45's already or can't be had without replacing the
  kernel; measured here (KVM guest, `tools/dev/kernel-check`), two
  settings gain with nothing given up, and Olo Doctor offers them:
  **full preemption** (a program woken while the processors are busy: 99
  in 100 within 4 µs where 950; the work itself unchanged) and **a limit
  on what waits in memory for a removable disk** (600 MB to a 10 MB/s
  stick: 14 MB unwritten at the copy's end where 280, on the disk 1.5 s
  later where 28 s). Measured and left alone: MGLRU's thrash protection
  (it ended a program that fitted in 3 runs of 9), dm-crypt without its
  work queues (a trade), split-lock mitigation, the watermark.
  Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ **Kernel** shows and switches those two
  and Olo's own pieces (BBRv3, the graphics-memory patch), each with its
  figures; `olo-doctor --kernel` is the same for agents. Kernel updates:
  the start argument goes into what a new kernel's entry is made from,
  and Doctor repairs an entry without it; both modules are built again
  at a new kernel's first start, and were built and run on Fedora's
  next kernel (7.3.3) in the guest, BBRv3's full self-check included;
  `tools/dev/kernel-next` does that for whichever kernel comes next.
  **For Ben**: after the upgrade, Olo Doctor shows "A program woken
  while the processors are busy waits for the kernel's tick" (Preempt at
  Once) and "A removable disk's writes pile up in memory" (Limit
  Removable Disks); the tab is Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Kernel. Run
  `tools/dev/kernel-next` when Fedora has a new kernel series (a series
  BBRv3 passes on goes into kernel/bbr3/CHECKED).

- **A Network Speed Test app** (Ben, 2026-11-16: "also with the BBRv3
  work add a new olo native Network Speed Test app that show not just
  total up/down but also all the advaned metrics/data about the
  connection that we are able to get"). *Done 2026-11-16* (HACKING,
  "Speed Test"): Speed Test (so renamed), among the apps. Download
  and upload over four connections each for eight seconds against
  Cloudflare's servers, with, live as it runs: the round trip idle and
  while the line is busy and what the busy line adds; what was sent
  again (the kernel's count going up, the server's own coming down) and
  what arrived out of order; the congestion control in use, its window
  and BBR's model of the path; how long the name, TCP and TLS took; the
  segment size; the link (Wi-Fi's band, rate and signal, or the cable's
  rate). `olo-speedtest --print` gives all of it as JSON. Tried on this
  line from a test screen: 677 Mbit/s down, 648 up, a round trip of
  9.6 ms idle and 86 ms while uploading with CUBIC (77 ms added: the
  queue BBRv3 is there to keep short). *For Ben, after upgrading:* open
  it from Deskbar's apps and press Start Test; try it before and after
  Doctor's "Use BBRv3" and compare "Added by a busy line".

- **Olo Doctor offers BBRv3 for TCP** (Ben, 2026-11-16: "i also want olo
  doctor to offer to set the tcp congestion control algo to BBRv3 if
  it's not. if BBRv3 is not shipped with fedora then vendor the kernel
  module/patches and adapt if needed and then have olo doctor take care
  of doing everything needed to switch to BBRv3"). *Done 2026-11-16*
  (HACKING, "BBRv3 for TCP"; kernel/bbr3/README.md). Fedora's `bbr` is
  BBRv1, and Google's BBRv3 is a kernel with patches to TCP; Olo carries
  it as a module for the kernel as it comes (`tcp_bbr3`, the congestion
  control `bbr3`: Google's source, what it needs of the patches made in
  the module), built, loaded and chosen at each start by `olo-bbr3`.
  Shown in a KVM guest running this computer's kernel
  (`tools/dev/bbr3-check`): every figure it reconstructs the same as the
  true one, and beside Google's real BBRv3 (a kernel built with its
  patches, for the guest) the same within the runs' spread on 15 links.
  On a 50 Mbit/s link with 40 ms of round trip: 45.8 Mbit/s to CUBIC's
  47.1, the round trip at 43 ms where CUBIC's is 69, and 0.03% sent again
  where BBRv1 sends 0.6%. *For Ben, after upgrading:* Olo Doctor shows
  "TCP could send with BBRv3" among its suggestions; **Use BBRv3** (asks
  for your password) builds the module and switches new connections to
  it. `sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control` then says `bbr3`, and
  `ss -ti` shows it on new connections. To go back:
  `sudo systemctl disable --now olo-bbr3.service`. It was not put on
  your computer's kernel by me: everything was tried in the guest.

- **Never a stall: the compositor's loop held in the kernel** (Ben,
  2026-11-16: "i just had a responsiveness stall when i was typing and
  it actually even repeated a letter eg "sunbursst" please root cause
  and fix", then "i don't ever want it stalling figure out how to make
  that happen … go as low level as you need to"). HACKING, "Windows'
  buffers stay in memory".
  - *The cause, fixed:* Intel's xe driver backed windows' GPU buffers
    up to swap whenever kswapd ran (a build's file cache is enough) and
    brought them back inside the next GPU submission, under locks
    app_server's every submission takes. Olo's live patch
    (`olo_gpu_memory`, kernel/gpu-memory) makes TTM's one gate say
    there's no swap for it; `olo-gpu-memory` (a root service) builds it
    for each kernel and loads it at every start; Olo Doctor installs it
    ("Keep Graphics Memory in Memory"), or turns swap off where the
    kernel can't take it. The same build: 47 slow frames (the worst
    951 ms) and three late keys before; none after, swap on.
  - *The core never swapped* ("keep all those core "responsiveness"
    processes out of swap always"): app_server (its input thread in
    it), the session, the supervisor, Deskbar, the proxy and the voice
    service lock their own memory as they start (`mlockall`, each page
    from its first touch: 3 MB more resident, 0.29–0.31 ms a frame
    either way); the sound server's three services are never swapped
    (`MemorySwapMax=0`). Doctor: "Keep the Core in Memory" (the
    account's locked-memory limit, now and at every login; the
    services' setting).
  - *Swappiness 1* ("maybe that combined with the swapiness to 1"):
    Doctor's "Keep Programs in Memory". Little either way once the
    patch was in (7.8 MiB swapped in 26 minutes of building at 60).
  - *Swap as large as memory, suggested* ("have olo doctor suggest a
    swap size equal to the ram size"): Doctor's suggestion, only where
    graphics memory is kept out of swap; it says what an empty one
    costs (a third of a percent of its size).
  - *Doctor offers all of it* ("make sure olo doctor will offer to
    configure all this automatically for the user if not already
    done"): four findings, each with its fix, each run for real here.
  *On Ben's computer now* (the fixes' own steps, as root, at his
  word): the patch in since 12:23, swap 62 GiB, swappiness 1, the
  limit raised, sound never swapped. *For Ben:* upgrade from Deskbar's
  tray: app_server, Deskbar and the session then lock their memory
  (Doctor says "The desktop's core keeps its memory from Olo's next
  start" until they have); and say if anything still stalls
  (`sudo tools/dev/gpu-holds` names what holds the loop). 1 GiB of
  buffers swapped out before the patch came back as their apps drew
  again, once each.

  xmonad, awesome, river, niri, Amethyst and yabai offer, set against
  Olo's auto-tiling, and what's missing made: layouts, their knobs, the
