- **From GPUI to Olo's own kits: retained, message passing, a looper a
  window** (Ben, 2026-11-10: "scrapping gpui in olo and replacing with
  our own beos inspired retained mode, smp first, message passing
  architecture … messages typed instead of dynamic … incredibly fast
  retained mode GUI … GPU rendering and SIMD everywhere it makes sense,
  avoiding CPU copies"; then "implement this change now, end to end, in
  full", with all documentation and an Olo Book, a guide for agents
  working on it, as the Be Book was). Measured first (release, the
  bench, 3456×2234 at 2×): GPUI's frames are 0.4–0.9 ms of CPU, a third
  of it laying out and painting what didn't change, and 1.1–2.5 ms of
  GPU, because every frame draws the whole window and says the whole
  surface changed (a caret's blink, a full-screen pass). What the new
  kits are for: work that follows what changed (a view tree, its layout
  and what each view drew all kept; only what changed drawn, and only
  that told to app_server), a window's looper never holding another's
  up, a display thread that scrolls and animates while a looper is
  busy, state changed only by typed messages on its own thread (no
  entity read while it's updated: there are none), and a tree agents
  read that is the view tree itself. GPUI's lower half, which is Olo's
  own work by now (the Wayland client, text, the renderer, the atlas),
  is kept. In stages, each leaving every app working:
  1. **The Application Kit** (`crates/app`, olo-app): loopers, handlers,
     typed messengers, timers, tasks, the worker pool, answers. *Done.*
  2. **The Interface Kit's core** (`crates/interface`, olo-interface):
     GPUI's lower half taken over; the display thread (the Wayland
     connection and the render stage: each window's display lists,
     scroll layers and damage); a looper a window; the retained view
     tree, layout and painting; input, focus, keys, text input; popups,
     layers, drags, the clipboard; the agent tree, frame marks, the
     layout review. *Done so far:* all of that but drags; scrolling on
     the display thread (the wheel and touchpad scroll there, elastic
     ends; `ScrollHandle`), rows made as they come near (`uniform_rows`),
     element state, window keys, held commits, window state, upgrade
     hooks; several damage rectangles a frame, a drawing made again
     damaged only where it differs (2026-11-13); drag and drop (a
     view's parts take drops, files dropped on an element), moving a
     window to another display (`on_move_window`), the layout lint's
     headless window, and agents' `Menus` by surface, `Move`,
     `WindowOver`, `WindowDropped`, `Focus` and `FocusIn` (checked
     2026-11-13). *Still to do:* pictures as elements (`img`) and
     animated ones; animations stepped on the stage; rows of
     differing heights (GPUI's `list`). *Done 2026-11-15:* a frame
     drawn straight from the kept drawings' glyphs, most of what a
     frame holds: a drawing's glyphs are shared once it's made
     (`Scene::seal`), the frame notes each run with where it goes, and
     the renderer puts each glyph in place as it copies it for the GPU
     (before, each was copied into the frame, then again into one
     sorted list, then to the GPU). StyledEdit full screen at 2×,
     scrolled (2,700 glyphs a frame; six rounds each in turn, release,
     medians): putting the frame together 42 → 18 µs, the frame 158 →
     131 µs. Quads and the rest are still copied (tens a frame).
     Same to the pixel (StyledEdit scrolled, Tracker, DeskCalc, the
     gallery; 1×, 1.5×, 2×, light and dark); damage-check the same (a flake
     of Terminal's at 1× it found, the build before's too, fixed the
     same day: a wheel's eased steps too small to show drew nothing,
     were taken for an end, and the notches' last pixel or so was
     dropped, as soon or late as the frames came; each step is a
     device pixel at least now). (A scroll bar's knob moved by
     the stage was looked at 2026-11-14 and left: every frame of a
     scroll draws the content it moves anyway, and the knob's own
     repaint is 0.02 ms of it.) *Done 2026-11-13:* nothing worked out or drawn
     for a layer surface stretched across its output, or a lock
     surface, before app_server has given it its size (they opened
     1 × 1 and were laid out and painted so once: the emoji picker
     16 ms of a 20 ms start that way).
  3. **The kit's widgets** on it (everything in olo-ui today). *Done:*
     theme, style, review, icons, cut, tip, keys, menu (bars, popups,
     context menus), agent, app (Frame, fits_content, kept sizes,
     upgrade), and the widgets control, buttons, views, text_field,
     text_control, menu_field, scroll, list, alert, status, key_hint,
     banner, find_bar, slider, tabs, side_pane, sidebar, color, thumbs,
     toolbar, text_view, charts, dashboard, slim_scroll: each pixel for pixel the same as olo-ui's at
     1×, 1.5× and 2×, light and dark (`tools/dev/kit-compare`, the
     `*_gpui` examples beside the kit's). Tips are `tip::on` everywhere
     (a popup under its widget, free of its window's edges; olo-ui's
     tool bar used GPUI's, at the pointer, inside the window). *Done
     since, as the apps that use them were ported (each with its app,
     stage 4), before olo-ui was deleted (stage 5, 2026-11-12):* strip,
     image_view, ruler; undo, spotlight, dnd, open_with, file_panel,
     search, code, brand, pictures, lock, copy, due, spell, lint (in
     `crates/kit`); workspaces (`olo_kit_base`); the editor
     (`olo_kit::editor`); `crates/preview`, `print` and `screensavers`
     (their `kit` views alone). Not ported: `part`, GPUI's cached view
     of a part of a window (so a change didn't draw the whole window
     again), needless where every view is retained and drawn again
     alone. (This list said "still to do" until 2026-11-14.)
  4. **Every app**, one at a time, each compared pixel for pixel and
     benched against its GPUI build before it moves. *Done:* DeskCalc
     (hover 0.3% of a core against 1.0%, typing 1.5% against 2.0%, the

     nothing at any scale in any window, light or dark. What agents
     read is the same (a secret's dots, never its value). *Measured*
     (release builds that take the test PAM service, 2×, 508 items,
     old → new): at rest 0.0% both; a frame as the arrows go down the
     list 1807 → 810 µs, the list scrolled 1192 → 319, a search typed
     1520 → 1369, a code counting down 851 → 346, the pointer over an
     item's fields 1059 → 620, typing in the editor 1923 → 318;
     resident 104 → 106 MB at rest, 105 → 108 after. (An item's
     details coming in no longer has the list and every filter worked
     out again: the arrows were 1101 µs before that.) *Differences,
     meant:* the item pane's scroll bar is there as a long item opens
     (it came with the first scroll); "Synced a minute ago" counts the
     minutes by itself; Escape closes Sync Problems and ⌘N works
     after an editor is cancelled (nothing had the keyboard); the
     list loses its focused look at once when the editor takes the
     keyboard; Sync Problems' icons are level with their items at 1×.
     *Found on the way, in the kits:* what hears a scroller wasn't
     told of one laid out for the first time, so a bar that shows only
     while there is something to scroll came with the first scroll;
     the review took a scroll bar's arrow for what follows a form's
     Save, and a thin level bar's edges for crowded lines. *For
     tests:* `onepassword-fake --items N`, `olo-keychain-ask`. *Not
     tried:* Touch ID, a security key and a look (a test session
     leaves the readers alone), a real 1Password, Chrome's extension,
     the SSH agent signing, the auto-lock's time passing, a link's
     value opened (it starts a browser), several accounts, Reset, on
     an agent screen (what's shared with it).
     **Terminal** (2026-11-11): one `Terminal` behind a lock, each
     window a view that has it say what it shows, a terminal window's
     screens a view of their own so a shell's output draws them alone
     (HACKING, "Terminal", "On olo-kit"). For it, in the kit: the
     grouped tab strip (`widgets::strip`, one drawing with its state in
     the element's own), a window of the app moved over another's
     strip (`WindowOver`, `WindowDropped`), `agent::invoking`, and a
     program that has quit running on, asleep, for what it copied
     (`olo_interface::before_lingering`: every kit app's, as GPUI's
     did). Old against new, each in a session of its own with its own
     olo-termd and a scratch home: output, colours, box drawing and
     emoji, a long output, the scrollback by the wheel (a notch, five
     at once), typing back to the end, a selection dragged, single,
     double and triple clicks, copy and paste, every menu, the screen's
     and a tab's menus, tabs made, hovered, chosen, dragged along the
     strip, undone, torn off into a window and let go on another's
     strip, Tile All Tabs, a pane picked, a divider dragged, Find and

     Dark, the Group window (a name, a colour), a group's menu, a busy

     a wrong one, the right one, Escape, Cancel, the close box), a
     working agent's badge and Keep It Going ▸ Custom Message…: the
     same to the pixel at 1×, 1.5× and 2×, light and dark, but for
     what is meant below. The review: nothing at 1×, 1.5× and 2× in
     any of them (sudo's at 1.25× and 1.75× too).
     *Measured* (release, 2×, back to back on a busy machine, old →
     new): at rest 0.0% both; a frame with twenty lines a second
     printed 532 → 305 µs (1.6 → 1.2% of a core), typing 475 → 240 µs
     (2.0 → 1.6%); the scrollback scrolled 539 → 292 µs; three panes
     printing 580 → 366 µs; a flood (`seq 1 3000000`, three takes): the
     same time to print (1.12 → 1.06 s) and the same CPU (1.19 → 1.19

     rest. *Differences, meant:* the
     cursor stays solid, and the program isn't told the window lost

     *Found on the way, in the kits:* an element that
     takes the keyboard on a click (`track_focus`) and hears nothing

  8. **AirPlay: send a window, a workspace, an agent screen or a video
     file to an AirPlay display** (Ben, 2026-11-12: "after this work
     please add airplay support to olo so that i can broadcast/stream
     either a specific window, a specific workspace, an agent screen or
     a video file to an airplay compatible display/receiver. it must
     support high quality video and audio"). After the kits' work
     (items 5 to 7). Native, as everything is (no wrapped tools): find
     receivers (mDNS, `_airplay._tcp` and `_raop._tcp`), pair and set
     up (AirPlay 2's HomeKit pairing where a receiver wants it, the
     older FairPlay-less paths where it doesn't), then two ways to
     send. *Mirroring* for a window, a workspace or an agent screen:
     what app_server's capture already hands the portal and Screenshot
     (`capture.rs`: a window, a display, a headless screen's frames as
     dmabufs), encoded H.264 or HEVC on the GPU (olo-video's NVENC,
     olo-vaapi) at the receiver's size and rate, with the sound that
     goes with it (the session's output, or the window's own stream)
     as AAC or ALAC, kept in step with the picture. *A video file* is
     better sent as itself where the receiver plays its format (the
     receiver fetches it from a server Olo runs for the length of the
     play: its own picture and sound, never re-encoded), mirrored
     through the Viewer's player otherwise. Where it's asked for: a
     window's tab menu and the Viewer (Send to ▸ the receivers found),
     Deskbar for a workspace, Agent Screens for a screen; a tray item
     while something is being sent, with Stop. Agents the same
     (`olo-airplay list|send|stop`). To find out first: what today's
     receivers (Apple TV, AirPlay 2 televisions, HomePods for sound)
     accept from a sender that isn't Apple's, since "high quality"
     depends on which path they allow; tests against a receiver of
     the test's own on a private network, never the person's.
     *Found out, 2026-11-12* (from what's published; nothing was run
     against a receiver), and it decides the design, so **waiting for
     Ben** on the two questions below:
     - *Mirroring as Apple's devices do it is closed to Olo.* AirPlay
       2's mirroring begins with a FairPlay exchange (`fp-setup`)
       whose sender's side is Apple's own. What's open is the other
       end: receivers that pass for an Apple TV (UxPlay, RPiPlay, the
       shairplay crates, with the "playfair" code). The one open
       sender for a Wayland compositor found
       (rabits/wlroots-airplay-screen-mirror) speaks the first
       AirPlay's mirroring, unencrypted, without sound, to MiraScreen
       dongles, and says of AirPlay 2 "w/o fp-setup". So low-latency
       mirroring to an Apple TV or a licensed television isn't to be
       had.
     - *Playing a URL is open, and is the high-quality path.* The
       sender asks the receiver to play an address and the receiver
       fetches it and decodes it itself: a file's own picture and
       sound, untouched. pyatv does this to Apple TVs today ("AirPlay
       play URL (including local files)"), after pairing once with a
       PIN the television shows (Apple TV 4 and later ask for it).
       tvOS 26.2 is reported to answer its status question with an
       error (pyatv issue 2821, open, a fix proposed): to be watched.
     - *So, the design:* a video file is played as itself from a
       server Olo runs for the length of the play. A window, a
       workspace or an agent screen is sent the same way, as a live
       stream (HLS: what capture hands over, encoded on the GPU as
       recordings are, with the session's or the window's sound as
       AAC, in segments the receiver fetches). That is full quality
       with sound, and it is **seconds behind** (a segment or two):
       right for showing a film, a presentation, an agent at work;
       not for pointing at something while talking, nor for playing.
       All of it native: mDNS, HomeKit's pairing (SRP, Ed25519,
       X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305), the HTTP server, the segmenter.
     - *Begun 2026-11-12: finding the receivers* (HACKING,
       "AirPlay"): `crates/airplay` asks by mDNS itself and reads
       what each receiver says it is and takes; `olo-airplay list`.
       On the network Ben's computer was on that day it found 28 in
       three seconds (Avahi, listening longer, 32): Apple TV 4Ks of
       three generations (`srcvers` 960 and 1005), Macs, one
       television with AirPlay built in; every one plays video, shows
       screens and asks to be paired with first (its flags' "pair
       once" bit). So the first question below is answered in kind
       (Apple TVs and Macs, all wanting HomeKit's pairing), though
       not which one is his: a shared network, and only he pairs, at
       the screen.
     - *Then the pairing, 2026-11-12* (HACKING, "AirPlay"):
       pair-setup with the code the receiver shows, pair-verify at
       each connection, the enciphered channel after it, and the
       pairings kept in a file only the person reads
       (`olo-airplay pair|check|paired|unpair`). **Never yet tried on
       a real receiver**: tests pair with one of their own, and the
       first real one is Ben's to do at its screen: `olo-airplay
       list`, then `olo-airplay pair "ITS NAME"` and the code it
       shows; `olo-airplay check "ITS NAME"` then says whether it
       knows the computer. What it says if it fails is what's needed
       to fix it. The keys could move into Passwords.
     - *Then a film played by its address, 2026-11-12* (HACKING,
       "AirPlay"): `olo-airplay play "ITS NAME" film.mp4` (or an
       address on the web; `--from 1:02:03`; Ctrl-C stops it there).
       The receiver fetches the file from this computer, by ranges,
       for the length of the play, and plays its own picture and
       sound. Reading on found that **today's tvOS no longer takes
       pyatv's released way** (26.2 answers `/playback-info` with
       500, 27.0 with 403: pyatv issues 2821 and 2906), and that the
       way it does take (commands on a stream of their own, state by
       events: pyatv's pull request 2846 and its rework, reported
       working on tvOS 26.5 and 27.0, Apple TV 4K of the 2nd and 3rd
       generations, and a 2025 Samsung) is unmerged there; Olo does
       the newer way first and the older where a receiver doesn't
       take it. **Never yet tried on a real receiver** (tests play to
       one of their own, both ways): Ben's to try after pairing, with
       `--trace` so that what a real one answers is seen. What a
       receiver doesn't play by itself (Matroska, WebM, AVI, Ogg) is
       refused with the reason.
     - *Then what shows while one plays, 2026-11-12:* each play says
       how it goes (`olo_protocol::airplay`), `olo-airplay playing`,
       `stop`, `pause` and `resume` act on plays from anywhere, and
       Deskbar's tray has a screen with a play mark while a film
       plays, its menu Pause (Resume) and Stop.
     - *Ben, 2026-11-12:* "for the airplay stuff please add the
       proper gui integration with a preferences panel, integrated
       airplay from relevant app menus and by right clicking the
       window title / deskbar row / workspace etc. cli alone is not
       enough". So, **next, in this order:** (1) Preferences ▸
       AirPlay: the receivers found, Pair… with the code a receiver
       shows, Forget, and what plays now; (2) "Play On" where a film
       is at hand: the Viewer's and Tracker's menus (a file's
       context menu too), the receivers paired with as its items;
       (3) sending what's live, which needs the live path first (what
       capture hands over, encoded on the GPU, as HLS the receiver
       fetches, with the sound that goes with it): a window from its
       title's menu and its Deskbar row, a workspace from its heading
       in Deskbar, an agent screen from Agent Screens, each "Send to
       ▸ a receiver", with Stop where it was started and in the
       tray. The command stays the way under all of it (and for
       agents).
     - *Low latency, 2026-11-12* (Ben: "see if there's a way to get
       low latency airplay working … i want video and audio";
       HACKING, "AirPlay"): not HLS but AirPlay's own mirroring, as
       doubletake (LGPL, Go) has found it works with today's Apple
       TVs: over a HomeKit pair-verified connection the picture and
       sound are keyed from the pairing, so **no FairPlay** is
       needed (the objevovat FairPlay-SAP code Ben pointed at is
       Apple-derived tables under the LGPL, and its README says both
       Apple TVs it was tried on refused it; Olo is MIT, so bringing
       any of it in is Ben's to decide, and nothing needs it now).
       `olo-airplay show` sends a window, a display or an agent
       screen with its sound, 8 ms from capture to sent,
       a lead of 40 ms wired (75 on Wi-Fi) at the receiver.
     - *The desktop's way to it, 2026-11-12* (HACKING, "AirPlay" and
       "Show on AirPlay and Play On"): Preferences ▸ AirPlay (the
       receivers, Pair… with the code typed, Check, Forget, Show
       Display, Stop); Play On ▸ in Viewer and Tracker for a film;
       Show on AirPlay ▸ in a window's tab menu, Deskbar's app rows,
       Agent Screens' Screen menu and Deskbar's agent screens item;
       the tray says a showing, with Pause and Stop. All tried on a
       headless session against the test receivers.
     - *A workspace, 2026-11-12* (HACKING, "Screen sharing" ▸
       Workspaces): Olo's own Wayland protocol makes a capture source
       of one of a display's workspaces, live though the display
       shows another (its windows where they were left, drawing on);
       `olo-airplay show --workspace N`, and Show on AirPlay ▸ on
       Deskbar's workspace headings.
     - *Frames fitted by app_server, 2026-11-12* (HACKING, "Screen
       sharing" ▸ Fitted): a busy screen shown costs olo-airplay 13.7%
       of a core, not 32.4%, and 4.7 ms from capture to sent, not 8.1.
     - *Frames kept on the GPU, 2026-11-12* (HACKING, "AV1 and H.264
       on Intel's and AMD's GPUs" and the showing): H.264 through
       VA-API (`olo_vaapi::H264`, its parameter sets written by us,
       quality 18 with a cap: 46.7 dB in 199 KB where NVENC kept 46.4
       in 322), frames lent to it by app_server as dmabufs: a busy
       screen shown costs olo-airplay 5.0% of a core rather than
       NVENC's 11.9%, the NVIDIA GPU asleep, for 7.3 ms from capture to
       sent rather than 4.7. Recordings take it too (`--encoder
       vaapi`, Preferences ▸ Graphics' Format).
     - *The sound on the television only, 2026-11-12* (HACKING,
       "AirPlay", the showing): an output of the showing's own,
       made in process, and the sound that goes with what's shown
       moved to it: a window's app's, an agent screen's programs', a
       display's the computer's; back where it was when paused or
       ended, by WirePlumber when killed. Half the cost of the monitor
       recording it replaces (2.3% of a core against 4.4% with sound
       playing).
     - *The television's own volume, 2026-11-12* (Ben: "yes use tv"):
       the volume keys set the receiver's volume (AirPlay's `volume`
       parameter, from the computer's at the start, as it changes),
       the sound sent at full scale. Tried on the test receiver; a
       real television is the test of how it takes it.
     - *The encoder, 2026-11-12* (Ben: "stay with intel"): Auto keeps
       Intel's VA-API H.264 on mains too (2.6 ms more from capture to
       sent than NVENC, inside the 40 ms lead; less than half the
       processor; the NVIDIA GPU asleep). `--encoder nvidia` stays.
     - *Ben's to say:* (1) which receiver it's for (an Apple TV and
       its tvOS, a television with AirPlay built in, something else):
       it has to be tried against the real one, paired by him at the
       television, since no test can stand in for Apple's end; (2)
       only if a real receiver refuses the mirroring without it,
       whether FairPlay is wanted (LGPL, Apple-derived).

     2026-11-11: "you can also remove GPUI and olo-ui as soon as you're
     done we don't need to wait for the coder and browser branches":

     `sum_tree` and `semantic_version`) are deleted; what olo-interface
     still uses of GPUI's helper crates and Blade is in `vendor/`
     (`vendor/README.md`, "From GPUI"); `crates/preview`, `print` and
     `screensavers` have only their `kit` views; `cargo ui-lint`, the
     hooks, bench, hdr-check, ui-lint, lockcheck and kit-compare know
     only the kits (`tools/reentry` and `lockcheck reentry` went with
     GPUI: a `Child` has one owner, so nothing reaches a view that's
     busy); the kit has its own `gallery`, `hdr_probe`, `hdr_card`,
     `lines`, `layer` and `book` examples and the two tests of olo-ui's
     it lacked; a frame's marks are right on olo-kit (where its
     scrollers were, marked when drawn, nothing left by a commit that
     drew nothing) and a view that scrolls itself says where it is
     (`Painter::note_scroll`: the editor, Terminal); HACKING.md speaks
     of the kits throughout (its GPUI mentions are history), and the
     Olo Book is `docs/OLO-BOOK.md`, its example
     `crates/kit/examples/book.rs`.
     *Measured against the build from before the kits* (`cc785d65`,
     built under /var/tmp/olo-pre; the whole benchmark at 2× on each,
     by what each step cost the process, 2026-11-12): the kits use 88%
     of its processor time overall (scrolling 80%, typing 76%, an idle
     second 52%, tabs 62%, menus 93%, a live resize 98%; the gallery
     39%, Notifications 70%, Logs 78%); a click to a menu's picture
     takes what it took (4 ms, Tracker's and Deskbar's).
     *Left* (then "The kits' costs, in absolute terms", done
     2026-11-16; each within a frame's budget):
     - A whole window drawn again every frame: the looper paints each
       node's drawing, the display thread copies them into the frame,
       then draws. A list-heavy window resized live: Logs 95 ms for 36
       steps, Notifications 195, Tracker 43; a drawing that moves
       every frame: StringTheme 70 ms for 210 frames (two threads
       woken, the drawing copied once more).
       To try: a drawing that's the only thing changed handed to the
       frame without the copy; `Scene::append` moving a recording
       whose clip holds all of it without looking at each thing in it;
       `finish` swapping the glyphs' list in when the runs are in
       order already; a list's rows of text keeping their recordings
       when only their width grew.
       Where a frame's time goes (Logs resized live, 2×, 40 frames,
       `OLO_FRAME_PHASES=1`, 2026-11-12): the looper 1.39 ms (the
       views' bodies 0.35, layout 0.24, painting 81 of 108 nodes
       0.80: some 2,900 glyphs recorded again though no row's text
       changed, nothing shaped or rasterized), the display thread
       0.41 (putting the recordings in the frame 0.19, drawing 0.19),
       and some 0.4 ms a frame that neither counts (2.2 ms a frame
       by the process's own time).
       *Followed further, 2026-11-12* (perf, which does work for a
       program it starts itself, and `tools/dev/memhist`: HACKING,
       "Whose time it is"): a quarter of a resize frame was libc's,
       copying and allocating, and most of that was the kits' own
       waste, now gone (a 3 KB shaped line copied twice a label, an
       allocation a `font()`, a line's text copied for every cache
       lookup, a drawing's lists grown from nothing at every
       repaint). Before and after in turn, three runs each, by cycles
       a resize step, the middle run [the least]: Notifications'
       history 17.1 [16.4] → 14.5 [12.9] million, Tracker on 3,000
       files 5.0 [4.3] → 4.2 [4.2], StyledEdit on 100,000 lines of
       code 10.3 [9.2] → 9.4 [9.4]; the same to the pixel in 36

       *And then, the same day:* a kept drawing's orders by what's
       over what (a draw a kind, not a draw a change of kind: Tracker

       cutting each thing, menus' shortcuts looked up, the standard

       that: the looper put each of 1,400 into the drawing again, the
       display thread compared each with the last drawing's, field by
       field, and then looked at each to take what falls in the part
       drawn. Now a line painted from what it kept goes into the drawing
       whole, says how it was made, and is compared and passed over a
       line at a time (HACKING, "Fast and light"); Terminal no longer
       looks through every glyph for colour emoji. Instructions, three
       rounds each in turn, 25 s of the spinner: 480–490 M → 231–233 M
       (the display thread 180 → 43 M, the looper 231 → 118 M); the
       display thread's comparing and per-glyph copying, 41 M of its
       361 M cycles, gone; a frame's assembly 0.011–0.016 → 0.006–0.010
       ms. The cycles moved within the noise of a machine busy with
       other work (−11% to +0.4%): what is left is memory and the
       driver. `tools/dev/damage-check` (new) finds each app's last
       picture the same drawn by its damage and drawn whole, at 1×,
       1.5× and 2×. *Left of it:* the looper still wrote every line's
       glyphs into each drawing (157 KB an update for a screen of
       text, read across cores). *Done after, 2026-11-14:* drawings
       share a kept line's glyphs (`Scene::insert_kept_run`, an `Arc` a
       line), put in place only where a frame draws them; the spinner,
       three rounds each in turn, 25 s: instructions 218–220 M → 174–176
       M (perf record by thread: the looper 142 → 91 M, its writing of
       the glyphs, 43 M, gone; the display thread the same, ~60 M);
       memory steady through the run (82 MB). damage-check the same at
       1×, 1.5× and 2×; Terminal's Edit menu (disabled items, drawn
       faded) the same to the pixel as before at each. The display
       thread wakes three times an update: the commit; app_server's
       release of the last buffer, as it takes the new one; and the
       frame callback, a moment later. The release could come with the
       callback, one wake fewer for every app's every frame, but at
       about 10 µs a wake (1.5% of the spinner's cost) it isn't worth
       holding every client's buffers longer (Chrome's, games',
       double-buffered programs' that would wait for one). And
       Terminal's screens' view says what it shows again for each
       output (0.03 ms: its elements, listeners and scroll bar made
       again), where its drawing alone is new.
       *Done after, 2026-11-14:* each update went through Terminal's
       own thread (the shell's output thread told it, it told the
       window): now the output thread tells the window drawing the tab
       itself (`Session::drawn_in`, set as screens are drawn), and
       Terminal's thread only hears that titles are due a look, at
       most every 400 ms. The spinner, three rounds each in turn, 25 s:
       that thread 381 → 146 wakes and 24 → 8 ms; all of Terminal's
       threads 2,256 → 2,029 wakes; instructions the same (218 M).
       Tested: a tab printing while hidden, shown again (current, and
       going on), tiled beside the active tab, moved to a new window.
     - Scrolling fails the benchmark's evenness now and then in both
       builds (a frame skipped in a drag or a glide), and the
       Viewer's live resize its budget in both. Looked into
       2026-11-12 with Notifications' history (3456 × 2234 at 1.5×,
       120 Hz, the Wayland messages timed): in the cycle of a skipped
       frame app_server sends the scroll's step and no frame
       callback. It holds a commit until its buffer's GPU work is
       done (`shell/mod.rs`, the dmabuf gate), and a frame whose
       work isn't done by the next tick gets its callback a tick
       late: on a GPU shared with the live desktop and other
       sessions, as the benchmark's is. Under the same load, ten
       drags each, back to back: the build from before the kits
       skipped 73 frames (0 to 23 a drag), the kits 7 (0 to 2). So
       it isn't the kits'; what's left is to run the whole benchmark
       with the machine to itself (it never was, the night it was
       measured), and to see whether a client can be told to draw
       while its last frame's GPU work is still finishing.
     *Found by the benchmark at three scales, and fixed, 2026-11-12*
     (HACKING, "Fast and light", the frame that waits for input's
     answer): a wheel's notch in the editor and Terminal drew one
     frame, 180 ms late, with a core busy (the frame's hold and the
     wheel's ease fed each other: the ease makes a step a display
     frame now, the hold lasts 4 ms from the first input not yet
     answered and a timer ends it); a scroll step shown a frame late
     while a document was still being laid out (a worker's commit
     taken for the answer: input is numbered and a commit says how
     far the looper had got); the checker took a glide's last pixels
     at 1× and 1.5× for hitches (two frames' worth in one frame, of
     a view that draws only when what it shows moves). The scrolling
     apps at 1×, 1.5× and 2× afterwards (174 steps, the machine
     busy): 7 fail, each a frame or two skipped or one of 9 ms, as
     above; before the fixes 21 of 465, every editor and Terminal
     scroll among them.
     - A window's making blocks its opener's looper while the display
       thread makes the surface and renderer (2 to 3 ms of a menu's
       4): the looper could build the view meanwhile. Measured
       2026-11-13 on Tracker's menus (`window made in`, median 1.88
       ms, 1.5 to 3.1): the Vulkan surface and its swapchain are 1.4 to
       2.3 ms of it, everything else 0.1 ms, and the opener's own work
       on the popup 0.3 ms; making the swapchain later would save only
       that 0.3 ms, so it wasn't done.
     Also left:
     *Done 2026-11-12:* the vendored Smithay asked winit for its
     "x11" feature, which built winit-x11, x11rb and x11-dl into
     app_server itself (not only its tests, as was thought): winit is
     Wayland alone now, and no X11 crate is in any build
     (`cargo tree -i x11rb`: none; the name stays in Cargo.lock as
     Smithay's optional dependency for a backend nothing turns on).
     `vendor/gpui-macros` is the style helpers alone (GPUI's macros
     for actions, `Render`, contexts, tests and the inspector, 1,300
     lines, removed), generating `crate::` paths, so olo-interface's
     `extern crate self as gpui` is gone too.
     *For the Book, learned porting (each cost a bug):* a drawing only
     looks (`Cx::canvas(|v: &V, g, b|)`): what it lacks it asks of its
     view by a message, and what it finds (where something went) goes
     in a `Cell`; lay out in `body`, for the width
     `on_bounds_changed` says, and draw what `Painter::visible_bounds`
     shows, with a `paint_key` so work below the view draws nothing;
     work that goes on with nothing to draw runs on a timer
     (`Cx::after_do`), never `on_next_frame` (no frame comes to a
     window that drew nothing); a pointer's place in scrolled content
     is `cx.listener_bounds()`, a drawing's own bounds are where it's
     laid out; a parent that says something of its child (a title, a
     tool bar, menus) hears it as an event the child emits when that
     changes, since the parent's `body` doesn't run with the child's;
     `ViewRef::update` runs later and reaches a view in another window
     of the looper, `Child::update` runs now; a scroll asked for as the
     content's size changes is `set_offset_once_laid_out`; windows of a
     document's own are `open_window_here`, documents' windows
     `open_window`, with the app's looper (a `Hub`) told through the
     proxy; test old against new with the pointer moved off, then
     look at one shot of each batch: the same to the pixel can be the
     same failure. A drawing's place is the bounds it's handed,
     never what a pointer handler last kept (nothing has moved over a
     window just opened); what's shared between windows is behind a
     lock in an `Arc`, each window keeping a flag the app reads (a
     save under way) rather than the app reading its views; a window
     the app must outlive (an error for a file that wouldn't open)
     is opened before the one it's about is closed, or the app ends
     between them; a test that drives a file panel types a name, not
     a path, and checks the file is there before believing the shot.
     An app that runs with no window keeps its state behind a lock
     the windows' views take to say what they show and to act
     (Passwords): never taken while it's held (a handler takes what
     it needs, lets go, then calls the kit), what's drawn later (a
     list's cells) drawn from what the view kept, and what the app
     wants of a view's own things (a field emptied, the keyboard
     moved) left as asks the view takes in `body`. `olo_kit::quit`
     ends the program at once: one that must outlive its windows a
     while (a copied secret) closes them, stays resident and quits at
     its own time. What reads differently as time passes ("a minute
     ago", a code's pie) wakes its own view for it (`Due`): nothing
     draws again by itself. What must hold after an event is over
     (which field has the keyboard, once a press beside it has taken
     it) is decided in `body` after an `invalidate`, not in the
     event's handler. A test session keeps what its app kept between
     starts; Return on a list opens things (a browser, in a test):
     press it only with the alert up; a difference from the old
     build may be the old build's (look before fixing).
     An app whose windows trade what they hold (Terminal's tabs)
     keeps one state behind a lock too, and its windows' own things
     (a text field, a list) are made by the window's view from what
     the app asked for as it opened the window (`FieldSpec`), their
     text read back through a copy the view keeps current, never a
     password's (the view says it only as it's sent). What draws
     often (a screen's output) is a view of its own, so the rest of
     the window (menus, a strip) isn't said again for it. What turns
     or fades by the clock asks to be drawn again from its drawing
     (`paint_again_within`), not by a timer that redraws the window.
     A widget that is one drawing keeps where it put things in its
     element's state as it draws, and its handlers go by that. Test
     keys after a click, not only before: the keyboard's place is
     what a click changes. What's fed faster than frames (a shell's
     output) is invalidated for the frame (`invalidate_at_frame`),
     and its cost measured where it's fed fastest (a flood, by the
     process's own CPU time around it: `tools/dev/cost` starts too
     late for a burst) as well as steadily. Old against new at 1.25×
     and 1.75× too: a window a point short and a border's smear
     showed only there. Something that asks for a password is tested
     with a stand-in for what checks it (`OLO_SUDO_REAL`, a made-up
     password), behind a guard that runs nothing when the stand-in
     isn't the one in place. GPUI drew a window's whole view again
     whenever anything shown in it changed (a field typed in, a list's
     choice); a kit view says what it shows again when it's told:
     what a view shows by a child's state (a Save enabled by a field's
     text) needs the child's event (`subscribe`, `on_select`). A
     drawing that took the pointer itself in GPUI (`on_mouse_event` in
     its paint) only draws in the kit: its element has the listeners,
     and they go by where the drawing put things (a `Rc<RefCell>` it
     fills) or by `listener_bounds`. A name the old code used for a
     colour's green (`g`) is the painter's now: look for what a
     mechanical rename shadows. A port that compiles is compared
     before it's believed: a script that opened nothing compared two
     empty desktops and found them the same.
  *Finished* (every app on the kits, GPUI and olo-ui gone since
  2026-11-12). What became of what was left (2026-11-15): the restart
  after a protocol error gives up at the third in a row (547765822,
  HACKING, "No app may die of an upgrade"); the kit's three parity
  features aren't needed and aren't made, as `part` wasn't: pictures are
  drawn through the painter wherever they're shown (`paint_image`), the
  animated ones (Telegram's stickers) decoded on a worker and drawn once
  a frame when due, and the long lists of differing rows lay out their
  own (Telegram's conversation, Notifications' history, Logs) or are
  uniform (`uniform_rows`); the kits' costs were an item of their own
  ("The kits' costs, in absolute terms", done 2026-11-16). *Left for Ben:* the
  camera bubble (Record ▸ Show Camera: it turns the camera on).

- **Olo independent of GNOME, 100%** (Ben, 2026-11-15: "we should be
  100% independent of gnome and not rely on any of its services etc so
  please also make sure that is done after this"). Done, in an Olo
  session: nothing of GNOME's runs (checked on Ben's session: no GNOME
  Keyring, dconf-service, gvfs, GNOME portal backends or settings
  daemons), and nothing of Olo's starts or needs one. Olo's keyring
  always answers: the Preferences switch that handed programs' secrets
  back to GNOME Keyring is gone, the stand-in never starts it, the
  session no longer finishes starting one another login screen's PAM
  started, its items come over from its files natively, and Doctor no
  longer offers GNOME Keyring's PAM module and flags any GNOME Keyring
  running in an Olo session. Already Olo's own: dconf (olo-dconf),
  every portal interface (olo-portal, olo-secrets; none to GNOME's or
  GTK's backends), GIO without gvfs. What Olo still speaks of GNOME's is
  serving it for GNOME and GTK programs (`org.gnome.desktop.interface`
  settings, `org.gnome.SessionManager`'s inhibit, gcr's prompter
  protocol, `Olo:GNOME` in `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP` for Qt). Checked too:
  Setup's packages (`installer::plan::PACKAGES`) are none of GNOME's
  (Mesa, libinput, PipeWire, polkit, NetworkManager, the portal's
  frontend, AccountsService, …), and Olo's 63 release programs link no
  GNOME library (no GLib, GIO, GTK or libsecret: libc, xkbcommon, GBM,
  PipeWire, libinput, libseat, libudev, libpam, pixman,
  libdisplay-info, zlib, libelf). A Fedora without GNOME at all (a
  minimal install): `olo-installer --console` (2026-11-15, HACKING, "The
  Installer"), the plan in the terminal, sudo for the password, Olo's
  login screen chosen where there's none; PackageKit and dnf's service
  put in place first with one dnf call where they're missing (Ben chose
  it over a package manager of Olo's own), by the Installer and by
  Doctor ("Software can't be installed here", Install Them). Tried
  end to end on a minimal Fedora 45 in a VM (2026-11-15, HACKING, "The
  Installer"): the console installer, then Olo's login screen and its
  desktop; five things found on the way, each fixed (Wayland's server
  library, `semanage`, the computer starting to its console, GDM where
  there's none, the session not set). *Left for Ben:* nothing; a
  minimal kickstart for `installer-check` itself would keep it tried.

- **The desktop went blank and came back, 13:29** (Ben, 2026-11-15:
  "i think something just crashed my whole desktop went blank and then
  came back"). Found (read-only: the journal, the session's own log):
  app_server ended by SIGKILL at 13:29:23 (olo-session: "app_server died
  (signal 9)"), restarted at once, every app reconnecting with its
  windows. Not Olo's watchdog (it sends SIGABRT first and says so), the
  supervisor (it asks first) or the out-of-memory killer (nothing in the
  kernel's log). It came three seconds into a live layout lint (the
  pre-push hook, of an agent's push: a dozen headless sessions at once
  at normal priority on the same computer and GPU). The likeliest cause
  left is the kernel's realtime limit: app_server's loop is realtime
  under rtkit's hard 200 ms without sleeping; the guard puts it back at
  50 ms (it did at 13:13:49, during an agent's video exports) but can't
  while a thread is inside the kernel, a GPU driver's wait. Done: the
  live lint and everything it starts run at idle priority. Then (Ben:
  "there should never be short kill rule and we should NEVER drop
  priority down … olo doctor should just offer to fix it … a 30s limit
  … so if it is truly stuck it will get killed"; "give the olo
  supervisor thread(s) slightly higher priority"): realtime never
  through rtkit, set by Olo's programs themselves where the account lets
  them (Olo Doctor's Allow Realtime: `limits.d`, `rtprio 70`, no time
  limit, from the next login; without it, threads keep their nice);
  never put back for running long; a thread stuck 30 s without once
  sleeping ends its program with a report (31 s, the kernel's kill); the
  session's watchdog and the supervisor's look at 21, above every other
  of Olo's; the kept core as it was. *For Ben:* Upgrade, Olo Doctor ▸
  Allow Realtime, log out and in.

  N`); Size: Actual, 2× or 3× in the Save panel (`--zoom`). Measured on

  constant use (86 min of video) in 25 s. *For Ben:* Upgrade, then

- **Agent Screens ended as it exported a video** (Ben, 2026-11-15: "i
  just tried to export an agent screen to a video and agent screens app
  crashed"). Found (read-only: the journal, the dead process's exit
  status in /proc, rtkit's log): SIGKILL from the kernel, 0.3 s after
  the encoder started. The export ran on a thread started unnamed from
  the window's looper, so it took the looper's name (`w>Agent
  Screens`); as the Export Video panel closed and the window had the
  keyboard again, app_server made the program's `w>` threads realtime
  by name, the encoder with them; it never sleeps, the guard (which put
  back only the threads it knew of) left it running, and at rtkit's
  hard limit of 200 ms the kernel ended the program. (Ben's Tracker had
  two `w>Home` threads for one window: it happens in other apps too.)
  Now a registered thread marks itself (SCHED_RESET_ON_FORK, which
  threads it starts don't have) and app_server makes only marked ones
  realtime; the guard puts back whichever thread ran over, registered
  or not; the export's thread has a name of its own. Reproduced in a
  test (an unregistered thread made realtime spinning: the old guard's
  process killed, 137; now put back, the registered one untouched).
  *For Ben:* Upgrade, then export again.

  was done by the version before it, whose copy took only PNGs and no

  longer lists (one it lists but hasn't the file of stays chosen, the
  default drawn until it comes), and a session restarted into a
  version installed moments ago copies what comes with the programs
  again itself (`upgrade::sync_data`), so what an older version didn't
  know to copy comes with the upgrade, not the one after. *For Ben:*
  Upgrade (the session running now copies JPEGs and tiles already),
  then choose again.

- **Agent Screens' History empty** (Ben, 2026-11-14: "there is a bug in
  agent screens i can't see any history it's just empty"; his
  screenshot: the running screen v2-qa-integrations, "2,073 actions"
  in its header and at the filter bar's right, Kind All Actions, Result
  Any, Time All Time, no search, yet the Time / Action list empty; the
  player under the picture at its last action, "click 570 347", 145:37:40
  of 145:37:40). The count says the actions are there and the player
  can reach them, so the list isn't showing rows it has: find why (the
  list's model not filled, filled before the window's size was known,
  a filter that hides everything, rows of zero height, a virtual list
  scrolled past its end), fix it at the root, with a test that opens a
  screen's History with thousands of actions and checks rows show.
  Done (2026-11-14): not the list or its rows but its scroll position.
  A scroller's place is kept twice: by its looper (which makes the
  rows near it) and by the display thread (which scrolls it under the
  wheel and fingers and says where it got to, each word marked with
  the looper's last move of it, so a word from before that move is
  dropped as stale). The display thread lets go of a scroller its
  window's commit leaves out (a list on a tab that isn't chosen) and
  started it again at its top when it came back, while the looper
  still had it at the end, where it had shown the newest action: the
  rows were made there, none at the top where it was drawn, the bar
  at the end, and every word of it after, the wheel's too, carried an
  old mark, so the looper dropped them all and it stayed blank.
  History → Stats → History did it, on a screen with no new actions
  (a new one revealed it again, which is why it came and went).
  Now every scroll layer carries where its looper has it, and the
  display thread starts one it hasn't from there (and after an
  app_server restart too): any list on a tab, in any app. Kept fixed:
  `ui_lint_a_list_shown_again_scrolls_from_where_it_was` (scrolled,
  hidden, shown: the wheel moves it from where it was; fails without
  the fix). Checked in Agent Screens with 2,104 actions: History,
  Stats and back, rows there, the wheel scrolls. Ben: after upgrading,
  switch tabs on a screen's History and back.

- **Calls: echo and poor sound reported by the people Ben talks to**
  (Ben, 2026-11-14: "i have had reports that people hear echo and just
  generally poor sound from me i need it to be super good quality for
  calls"). *Found* (his journal, voice.json, ALSA, read only):
  - Olo's voice processing (echo cancellation, noise suppression,
    level) has been **off since 2026-11-09 12:36** (`voice.json`
    enabled false): every call since had the raw microphone, echo
    left to each call app.
  - Why it was likely turned off: on that day's call an app's
    automatic gain control (WebRTC's: its clipping step, 15 of 255,
    to its floor, 70) stepped the microphone down 71% → 29% in four
    minutes, because the service passed the source's volume on to
    the microphone and made up for it, so the app never heard its
    change take effect, while AGC2 made the loss up digitally, noise
    and all. **Fixed**: the source's volume is the app's, applied
    after the processing; mute stays shared; back to 100% after.
  - After its first call the service **never stopped**: the
    microphone stayed open and the noise model ran, 11.5% of a core,
    for good. **Fixed** (it follows the links from its source).
  - The built-in microphone's codec gain (`cs42l43 Microphone`) is at
    its top, +31.5 dB (PipeWire's 100%), with the DSP's compressor
    after it: loud speech and keys near the mics can clip there, and
    fan noise comes up with the voice. Not changed: it needs his
    voice measured.
  *Ben's:* upgrade, then turn Voice Processing on again (Preferences ▸
  Sound, or Deskbar's speaker menu, Clean Up Microphone Sound). Say
  what he calls with and through what (laptop speakers, the Studio
  Display, the TV over HDMI, AirPlay, headphones), and whether an echo
  test may run on his machine: speech played through his speakers and
  his microphone recorded for some seconds, in memory only, to measure
  the echo left and set the microphone's gain. Echo cancellation has
  never been tried on the real speakers (it's in "AirPods and voice
  processing, tried on the real things", below).

- **The pointer never stops under load** (Ben, 2026-11-12: "under
  load the mouse still gets unresponsive for a few seconds every now
  and then. i've got LAVD off b/c that made it even worse, as did the
  supervisor. how else can we improve desktop responsiveness even
  under load?", then "wouldn't it be better to give the cursor its own
  thread anyway?"). Looked at first, read-only, on his session: during
  a build (load 15–23) app_server's main thread waited at most 33 ms
  to run, but twice sat 78 and 142 ms inside an ioctl in the xe GPU
  driver's buffer lock (`drm_exec_lock_contended`), with the pointer
  stopped meanwhile; the freezes of seconds weren't caught. *Done
  2026-11-12:* app_server says in its log when input reaches it late
  and what held its loop (HACKING, "{"type":"timings"}"), so the next
  freeze names its cause; agent screens and test sessions no longer
  raise their app_server above everything. *Done 2026-11-13:* the
  pointer on a thread of its own (HACKING, "The pointer on a thread of
  its own"): Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Scheduler ▸ Pointer, "Move the
  pointer on a thread of its own", off until Ben has tried it. libinput
  is read on a thread at nice −15, which moves the hardware cursor
  itself when the loop hasn't taken a motion for 12 ms; the loop
  catches up from the same events. Tried on a real seat of the check's
  own (`tools/dev/cursor-thread-check`: vkms and a virtual mouse on
  "seat-olotest", his session never sees them): with the loop held
  400 ms, on the loop the pointer stood still 260 ms and ended at 162
  of 302 px (the kernel drops a device's unread events past 64); on the
  thread it never stood still more than 20 ms and ended where it
  should; switched on and off live, both ways. Costs nothing idle, and
  about 3% of a core more while a 1000 Hz mouse moves. *Ben's to try:*
  after upgrading, turn the switch on and use the machine under load
  as when it froze: the pointer should keep moving even when windows
  stop drawing. **Not tried on his machine**: his Intel panel (PSR2)
  may take the kernel's slow path for a legacy cursor move, which only
  it shows; if the pointer is worse with it on, turn it off and say so.
  *Found on his session, 2026-11-13* (read-only: its log and
  `{"type":"frames"}`): with the switch on, the loop was held 106 to 170
  ms three times while drawing, and the thread never took over, because
  on his OLED in HDR the pointer was never on the cursor plane: it was
  composed into the HDR frame, so every move was a compose and an
  encode on the GPU. *Done:* in HDR the pointer goes on the cursor
  plane, its pixels encoded into the PQ signal as they're copied there
  (HACKING, "HDR"); on a simulated HDR display (`cursor-thread-check
  --hdr`) the thread moved it 129 px through a 400 ms hold, and moving
  the pointer cost app_server 3.2–4.0% of a core where it cost
  12.4–15.3%. *Ben's to try after upgrading:* the pointer in HDR looks
  as it did (white as bright as a window's white, its edges clean), and
  `{"type":"frames"}` says `cursor_plane: true` for eDP-1.
  (LAVD is running again: an Authenticate dialog on his session, for
  `olo-doctor --helper`, started `olo-scheduler.service` on 2026-11-12
  at 22:44.)

- **A window on the HDMI display was scrambled** (Ben, 2026-11-12:
  "when i plugged in an hdmi cable earlier to try show a video on the
  tv the graphics/image was all messed up / scrambled. fix."). What it
  was is in HACKING ("Each display on its own GPU", "A window drawn by
  one GPU, shown by another"): the HDMI port is NVIDIA's, apps draw
  with Intel's, each window's picture is copied into a buffer both
  read, and NVIDIA's driver reads such a buffer as if its rows were the
  window's width rounded down to 8 pixels: sheared, a few pixels a row,
  at every width that isn't a multiple of 8. *Done 2026-11-12:* the
  copy is made with rows of a whole multiple of 16 pixels; a buffer
  NVIDIA would misread is never read by it directly; apps aren't
  offered linear buffers for NVIDIA's displays. Found and checked
  without a television, by `olo-app-server --probe-shared`, which
  draws on one GPU and composes on the other as the session does and
  compares, pixel by pixel: before, right at 1920 and 1408 wide and
  wrong at 964 and 333 (and at every width between multiples of 8, of
  91 tried); after, the same at all of them, for each kind of buffer,
  a picture replaced and a part redrawn (175 tries, none wrong).
  *Ben's to try:* after upgrading, plug the television in again and
  move a window to it (a film in the Viewer, a browser): it should
  look as it does on the panel. **Not seen on a television**: none
  was plugged in while this was fixed, so what the probe can't see is
  untried: the frames NVIDIA sends to the display itself (they were
  NVIDIA's own all along, and the wallpaper and the windows' frames
  there were its too), and anything else that was wrong with the
  picture that day. If it still looks wrong: which part (the whole
  screen, the wallpaper, or only windows), and
  `olo-app-server --probe-shared /var/tmp/shared` says whether the
  copies are still right.

- **DiskBackup** (Ben, 2026-11-07, after the work items before it):
  "build DiskBackup which is an olo native app and service for
  continuous, minimal impact (in terms of cpu/mem/network usage -- it
  should always just use background resources) full disk backups that
  are stored in the cloud (for now just build google drive storage
  support but do it in a way where we leave the door open to add more
  providers in the future). the app should automate all setup that
  needs to happen to connect to gdrive and start backing up there, and
  backups should be encrypted with a token/key that lives in olo
  passwords and the app should be able to restore from the target and
  the user can choose what to restore in an easy to use ux and it should
  also support versioning in a way that minimizes disk usage so only
  changes and deltas need to be kept and it should also compress
  everything. make sure it's all ultra efficient, background resources
  only, highly customizable with excellent defaults, it should include a
  deskbar widget too and the ability to run as a service so the app
  itself doesn't need to be open for backups to happen, and it should
  integrate with all the olo stuff in all the places that make sense. it
  should always provide very clear and transparent status about
  everything it's doing and has done. it should of course support
  excludes and it should have a bunch of built-in exclude
  groups/templates that cover e.g. all kinds of files that can be
  regenerated e.g. build/debug files for programming languages, node
  modules, downloaded cargo cache stuff and so on. also include
  integration with olo tracker so in olo tracker anything where the most
  recent version is backed up gets a slightly modified icon with a
  little green tick in the bottom right. and if you right click you can
  see older versions and restore them and so on. and everything has to
  continue to be super responsive and built to work great even with slow
  and awkward storage backends like google drive. and also obviously we
  should support files of any size and so on, handling all the plumbing
  needed to make this all work properly with any storage backend."
  To think through first: content-defined chunks (deduplicated across
  versions and files, compressed, encrypted, packed into large objects
  for a slow store), an index kept locally and in the store, a storage
  trait (Google Drive first: OAuth set up by the app, resumable
  uploads, rate limits), a service at idle priority (I/O and CPU) that
  follows changes (fanotify) rather than scanning, Doctor and Deskbar
  and Tracker and Passwords where they fit.
  Ben, later the same day: "make sure that i can also set a max
  upload/download speed for the backups too".
  Done: the engine (crates/diskbackup: chunks, packs, index, trees,
  snapshots, excludes, restore, speed limits, a folder as a store); the
  service and its command line (idle priority, a schedule, Back Up Now,
  Stop, battery, status, the key in the login keyring); HACKING.md,
  "DiskBackup"; the app's window (status, target and setup, the key kept
  in Passwords, folders, leave-out groups named by what they leave out,
  patterns, schedule, speed limits); restoring (a snapshot browser, put
  back where it was, Replace or Keep Both, or elsewhere); setting up on
  another computer (a backup there whose key this one hasn't: the keys
  Passwords keeps tried); keeping and tidying (snapshots past `Keep`
  forgotten after each backup, what only they used freed daily: packs
  deleted or copied from, locks so two computers or a restore never
  collide, trees in packs the cache keeps, the index checkpointed every
  five minutes; the app's Keep box); Deskbar's item (what it's doing in
  a glyph, its menu: Back Up Now or Stop, Pause, Restore Files…);
  Tracker's ticks (files backed up as they are now) and Older Versions…
  (DiskBackup's Versions window: Keep Both or Replace); Olo Doctor's
  checks (not set up, not running, paused, nothing for days, the key
  only here: each with DiskBackup's own fix); its own icon (a drive, a
  cloud with a tick before it), in every theme; Google Drive (each
  person's own Desktop app OAuth client, the app walking them through
  making it; resumable uploads, backoff, speed limits; tested against a
  Google of our own); a lost index healed (packs read back from their own
  lists, in tidying and before a backup). Left for Ben: go through Back
  Up To ▸ Google Drive… with a Google account of his (the steps' wording
  is from Google's current docs, not yet tried on the console itself),
  and choose where his own backups go. Following changes rather than
  walking: decided against (2026-11-08). fanotify's whole-file-system
  marks need root (CAP_SYS_ADMIN), and the service runs as the person;
  inotify needs a watch per folder (about 100,000 for a home, about a
  kilobyte of kernel memory each, past the default limit). An unchanged
  walk of 100,000 files takes 0.4 s at idle priority once an hour. A
  damaged index file is passed over and healed by itself
  (its packs read back from their own lists, named again, the file let
  go of when tidying).

- **Voice Processing's delay: Ben to choose the default noise model**
  (Ben, 2026-11-07: "we need that to be way more optimized so that it is
  not introducing any kind of noticeable lag"; "get rid of the remaining
  delay"). Done: 51 ms really (said 40) → what an app recording through
  Pulse gets now, measured with a synchronous probe: 30 ms with
  DeepFilterNet3, 10 with DeepFilterNet3 Low Delay (Preferences ▸ Sound
  ▸ Noise model), 0 with noise suppression off; the "cycle a source fed
  by another stream is behind" was the old probe's (pw-record is
  scheduled asynchronously), not Olo's. Left: Ben to choose the default
  once he's heard both (Try It compares them). tract allocates ~850
  times a frame on the realtime thread (each op's output tensors), but
  that costs nothing measurable (2026-11-08, DeepFilterNet3, 3 runs
  each): with mimalloc's thread-local free lists in place of glibc's,
  a frame back to back was 239-252 µs against 244-249, and paced every
  10 ms the median was 591-607 µs against 592-607, the tails noisy
  either way. A frame's time is streaming the weights, not the heap, so
  ops writing into buffers made once (a change to every op in tract)
  isn't worth it.

- **Intel's render GT on an idle desktop: not stuck** (Ben: "do intel
  gpu"). The 4 ms of rest a second first seen was a passing load. With
  Olo idle (a test session of its own, settled) the render GT rests as
  it did without it (816 ms a second against ~800: nothing measurable);
  on your desktop it rests ~800 ms a second, awake the rest because your
  displays draw 32, 12 and 13 frames a second as things on them change
  (agents' terminals, the clock): work following change. One thing to
  know: Performance mode puts Intel's GPU on Fastest, its lowest clock
  held at 1600 MHz (`/etc/olo/gpus.json`), so whenever it wakes it runs
  fast; Balanced and Power Saver don't. What it did find: app_server's
  100 ms look at resting displays (done since, 7af77a04: "A resting
  display still looked every 100 ms" in Done).

  2026-11-06: "build a polished, robust olo installer so that someone
  can download/install a stock fedora 45 then download the olo installer

  whole download-install-use process in a vm/qemu or somerhing"). One
  program downloaded from the public repository's releases, run on a
  stock Fedora 45 Workstation (GNOME, as it comes), full screen: a Setup
  in Windows 95's spirit (the deep blue gradient backdrop, the big
  title, the Welcome, Licence, Choose, Copying files with its progress

  and bevels, its fonts), saying throughout what it does and why. It

  Workstation install, the installer downloaded and run, a reboot into
  Olo, Olo used: its apps opened, a file opened, Preferences changed),
  screenshots of every step kept, at the VM's screen's scale and 2×.

- **Nothing of GNOME's needed: Olo's own in its place** (Ben, 2026-11-06:
  "if we are still reliant on any gnome services or settings, create olo
  replacements for it so we don't need any gnome stuff"). Done. Running
  in Ben's session were GNOME's portal (and gnome-control-center under
  it), GTK's portal, dconf-service and gvfs; GNOME Keyring started at
  each login. Each now has Olo's own:
  - **Portals** (ec3928a6; HACKING, "Screen sharing"): olo-portal serves
    Settings (the look, from the same list app_server writes to dconf)
    and Notification (into Olo's centre, actions back to the program);
    `olo-portals.conf` names every interface (`default=none`); the
    portal service is told the desktop is Olo alone (it read GNOME's
    configuration too, as the session says `Olo:GNOME`).
  - **dconf** (dcb59351; HACKING, "Other toolkits' programs"):
    `olo-dconf` answers `ca.desrt.dconf` with dconf's own interface and
    file (GNOME's `dconf dump` of a rewritten copy of Ben's database is
    byte for byte the same), named for D-Bus in the runtime folder while
    Olo runs; GNOME's stopped if it was answering.
  - **Keyring** (81b74430; HACKING, "Programs' secrets"): the login
    password opens Olo's keyring (`pam_olo_keyring` in olo-login's PAM,
    in `pam_gnome_keyring`'s place; olo-secrets keeps its key sealed by
    it, asking once after a face or fingerprint login or a password
    change); olo-secrets serves the Secret portal too (it didn't: Flatpak
    apps, Chrome and Slack asking the portal got nothing while it
    answered); Programs' Secrets is on by default; GNOME Keyring is read
    only when it's running or its keyrings changed.
  - **gvfs**: what Olo starts uses GIO's own files
    (`GIO_USE_VFS=local`), never exported, so GNOME keeps it.
  - **Olo Doctor** says when any of GNOME's services still runs, and
    quits them.
  Kept: `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=Olo:GNOME` (a name, not a service: Qt
  follows Olo's look only by it, toolbox programs too; the portal service
  alone sees `Olo`), the accessibility bus (at-spi, freedesktop's, which
  Olo reads programs through), and GDM until Ben switches to olo-login.
  Seen on Ben's machine: `gnome-browser-connector-host` runs while
  Chrome does, from Chrome's "GNOME Shell integration" extension (his to
  remove). To try: upgrade (the new portal setup and dconf take over at

- **Agents' tab title tool works by itself, always** (Ben, 2026-11-06,
  "i've asked you like 10 times to make the olo terminal set tab title
  mcp work properly and yet it still errors", "i don't want to have to do

  "have olo serve a localhost http server for it and have claude connect
  to that and olo keeps it available seamlessly on upgrades like we do
  with token pool … fix it right"). Why it kept failing: the tool was a
  stdio server each agent started, and Claude Code never starts a stdio
  server again once it has gone (its own code reconnects only HTTP and
  SSE servers); three were ended by signals on 2026-11-06 while their
  sessions went on, each tool lost till /mcp. Now the session serves it
  over loopback HTTP (`olo-terminal --mcp-service`, one of olo-session's
  services, at `http://127.0.0.1:17893/mcp`), and Terminal names that URL
  in Claude Code's and Codex's settings. No sessions kept, every request
  on a connection of its own: an upgrade execs the new version in place
  with the listening socket handed over (2235 requests from four threads
  through ten upgrades, none refused, `tests/title_service.rs`); a crash
  is restarted by olo-session and the agent's next call works (tried with
  Claude Code 2.1.319 itself: a call while it was down failed once, the
  next succeeded, the same session); `tools/dev/agent-title-check` drives
  Codex's way and Claude Code's, across an upgrade and a crash, headless.
  Left for Ben: upgrade. olo-session starts the service and Terminal
  rewrites the agents' settings by themselves; Claude Code sessions
  started from then on have it. One already running keeps the stdio
  server it started with (Claude Code doesn't read its MCP settings
  again), so one whose tool is already gone, as this session's is, gets
  it back when it's next started. Ben, 2026-11-06, still seeing "MCP
  server 'olo-terminal' has disconnected" ("i've asked you to come up
  with a solution/fix like 10 times. what's the deal?"): the service was
  answering; the session showing it began on 2026-11-05 at 09:18, before
  the move to HTTP, and four running then still had the stdio server
  they started with. Nothing in Claude Code reconnects those, so the
  title no longer depends on the tool: `olo-terminal --tab-title
  WORDS…` does the same from the agent's shell, and the hook (the
  installed binary, run with every prompt) names it for when the tool
  isn't there. Sessions already running pick that up from their next
  prompt after the upgrade, with no /mcp. Tried from this session (its
  tool gone): titled, from its folder and from another; outside a tab,
  it says so and exits 1.

- **Token Pool upgrades seamlessly** (Ben, 2026-11-06): "make it so that
  on an upgrade token pool app is seamless, i.e. it should serve new
  requests in the new process but allow old requests to finish in their
  existing process so that nothing errors". On an upgrade, the new Token
  Pool takes every new connection and request from the moment it's up,
  while the old one finishes what it's answering (streams included) and
  then goes; no request sees an error or a refused connection.
  *Done* (2026-11-06, HACKING's "Upgrades of the pool itself, without a
  gap"): a copy of the new version starts with the listening sockets and
  answers every new request at once; the old finishes its own (streams
  too) saving nothing, a sign-in renewed by either only once (the store's
  lock, read again first), then the pid olo-session follows stays as a
  keeper of the new copies (no restart, no error). olo-session no longer
  stops a program still finishing for an upgrade 90 s in (the kit's
  waiting marker); the gateway's own API counts its requests as under way
  too (a stream there used to be cut). Tested with a fake provider and end
  to end with real processes: a 20 s stream finished whole while new
  requests were answered in a second.

  2026-11-07: app_server restarting (an upgrade's reload, a crash) still cut
  every stream ("Connection lost mid-response"): the kit re-executed the
  pool at once when the compositor went. It now hands over first (35ee3e09;
  a tunnel across `tsession reload` broke before, held after). *Left*
  (Ben's upgrades, seen as they happen): the next upgrades on the
  machine with no agent's answer cut (the first may still be, run by
  the old pool).

- **Switching to olo-secrets broke gh's login** (Ben, 2026-11-06,
  urgent): "i tried switching to olo-secrets and now it broke everything
  and e.g. gh won't even auth" ("no token found for benmyles", then "The
  token in default is invalid"); "this has to just work seamlessly so it
  doesn't break like this next time and olo doctor needs to repair/heal
  it on the next upgrade"; "can you also heal my keyring for me right
  now". *Found*: two login keyrings, `login` and "Login" (Olo's own
  Secret Service client made "Login" beside GNOME's `login` on
  2026-11-04, when the new computer had no default alias), both copied
  in; and olo-secrets' `replace` matched attributes exactly where GNOME
  Keyring matches those given, so gh's new token went in beside the
  copied old one (which had GNOME's `xdg:schema`), go-keyring read the
  old one first, and gh's active-account item was in the other keyring.
  *Fixed*: olo-secrets answers as GNOME Keyring does (`xdg:schema`
  given, replace by the attributes given) and mends its store at every
  take-over (so every upgrade): the second login keyring merged in, each
  secret once, the newest first; Doctor says what it mended, offers Merge
  Them if two are ever listed, and says when GNOME Keyring has two; the
  hand-back and Olo's client use `login`. *Ben's keyring healed*
  (11:31): the store backed up (/var/tmp/olo-secrets-backup), the fixed
  olo-secrets installed and started again: "Login" merged, 2 duplicates
  gone; gh's active-account item set to the token of his 11:21 login, as
  gh's own login would have (nothing printed). *Then* (Ben: "did you
  fix it yet it still doesn't work"): gh still found no token, because
  `Item.GetSecret` replied with four values, not the spec's one struct
  (zbus makes a returned tuple several out arguments), which go-keyring
  can't read; Python and libsecret took it, so the replays passed.
  *Fixed* (one struct, checked on the wire and in the take-over test),
  installed again (store backed up), and gh's own login run with the
  token from his 11:21 login (piped, never shown): `gh auth status`
  says "Logged in to github.com account benmyles (keyring)".

- **Olo Doctor's "Voice processing's sound isn't realtime" comes back
  after Fix** (Ben, 2026-11-06): "i press fix it, it says it's fixed,
  but then it just comes back". *Found*: the fix did take (rtkit's
  journal: refusing every request for days at its default 15 processes,
  then restarted at 10:59:07 with 64 and 256, and olo-voice's sound
  thread made realtime at 10:59:17, the supervisor's next once-a-minute
  try); but Doctor looked again the moment the fix finished, still found
  the thread refused, and showed the finding again. *Fixed*: a fix can
  leave a step to do as the person before that look (`after_fix`); this
  one asks rtkit for the voice services' sound threads itself (rtkit
  gives only to a thread's own user, so not the root helper). Ben's
  thread is realtime now, so his next look shows it fine.

  in folder should show in tracker. basically every integration point
  we can do (whether cleanly through some protocol or 'dirty' through
  some hack) we should do so that everything feels as seamless as
  possible". Clean ways first (portals, D-Bus services, settings), a
  hack where there is none. Each is for Chrome, Electron (Slack,
  Discord, VS Code), GTK 3/4 and Qt 5/6 alike unless noted:
  - **File pickers** (started 2026-10-30: olo-portal answers the
    FileChooser portal with the kit's file panel, open, save and folder,
    several files at once, the app's filters by glob and MIME type as a

    tried. The toolkit switches are deliberately not set for everything:
    they also send GTK's link opening through OpenURI, which asks for an
    app until one was picked 3 times (HACKING, "Open and Save"); done

    FileChooser to it. Chrome and Electron use the portal with

    GTK 4 apps use it by default, GTK 3 with `GTK_USE_PORTAL=1`, Qt with

- **An app_server restart modesets every display** (seen 2026-11-01
  in the kernel log at each upgrade: apple-dcp `set_digital_out_mode`
  for each of the three displays, "Already set to timingID" yet done
  again: the screens freeze for a second or two per restart). The
  new app_server could keep a CRTC's mode when it is the one already
  set (the same mode blob, no ALLOW_MODESET commit) and go straight
  to page flips; where Smithay's surface init insists on a modeset,
  Olo's Smithay changes that. Until then upgrades of app_server are
  batched, not one a change. (Still: the kernel logged
  `set_digital_out_mode` 856 times in the day to 2026-11-02.)
  **Found** 2026-11-02: app_server opens each GPU with
  `DrmDevice::new(fd, true)` (udev.rs `device_added`), and Smithay's
  `disable_connectors` runs `reset_state`, switching every connector
  off: each display is modeset from dark at every start. The fix:
  open with `false`, and in Olo's Smithay let a surface take over a
  CRTC already showing its mode (`State`'s mode compared by timings,
  not the mode's type bits and name, which differ between a CRTC's
  mode and a connector's list), so the first frame is a page flip;
  switch off the planes the last app_server left on (a cursor or
  overlay plane still showing its buffer) in that first commit, no
  modeset needed; and if the driver refuses it, `reset_state` and
  modeset as now. It needs trying on the real displays (an upgrade
  the person agrees to try), so it isn't shipped blind.
  *Done, opt-in* (2026-11-06; HACKING's "The displays' modes at a
  restart"): `display.keep_modes: true` in app_server.json (or
  `OLO_KEEP_MODES=1`) opens each GPU without the reset, switches off
  only the last app_server's cursor and overlay planes (no modeset;
  refused, it resets as ever), keeps a CRTC's mode when it is the one
  asked for by its timings (unit-tested: a CRTC's mode and a
  connector's listed one, the kernel's equality telling them apart),
  and leaves the displays as they are when app_server goes. Off by
  default: untried on real displays (headless has no DRM).
  *Left* (Ben): set it, upgrade, and see the displays stay lit (the
  kernel log should have no `set_digital_out_mode` for the restart).

  highlighting** (Ben, 2026-11-05, lower priority): "when opening a
  markdown file StyledEdit should natively support the Markdown and be
  more like Typora WYSIWYG editing, but also have an option to switch
  back and forth between WYSIWYG mode and source mode and in source mode
  it should be like a code editor with syntax highlighting and fixed
  width font. also make it support code/source mode for all major
  programming/scripting languages with syntax highlighting and fixed
  width font." *Done* (2026-11-06): a `.md` opens as
  a Markdown document edited as it looks, Typora's way, its text the
  file's own Markdown (so it's saved as written: list markers, emphasis
  characters, line breaks, front matter, HTML): headings; emphasis,
  strong, struck; `code` on its ground; links; pictures (a file beside
  it, shown as the picture); bullets, numbers and task boxes hanging in
  their indents; quotations with their bar; code blocks shaded,
  labelled and coloured by their fence's language; tables as ruled
  grids typed in cell by cell (Tab to the next, Return adds a row);
  rules; front matter. The marks are hidden but on the lines the
  selection is on, where they show dimmed, as typed. Return goes on
  with a list (the next number, a task unchecked) or a quotation and
  ends it on an empty item; Font ▸ Bold, Italic, Strikeout, Code (⌘E),
  Link (⌘K) and Paragraph ▸ Body, Heading 1–6, Quote and the lists put
  the marks in. Document ▸ Show Source (⌘/): the same text as a code
  editor (monospaced, coloured, line numbers), caret, selection and
  view kept. Source code in 43 languages (`crates/syntax`: tree-sitter
  grammars in process, highlight queries mapped to the palette's token
  classes), a file going straight to it by its name, extension or `#!`
  line; Document ▸ Language to choose; Return keeps the indent, Tab
  types the file's own. All parsing on workers (a big Markdown
  document's and big code's once typing pauses), colours following
  edits meanwhile. In the kit: `olo_ui::code`, and the editor's line
  numbers, hidden spans, span grounds, paragraph shades, bars and
  rules, `Row::cells` and `Document::types` (HACKING: "Source code and
  Markdown"). Measured (release, 120 Hz, bench's new

  2.2 MB): launch 76–80 ms, scrolling p99 1.1–1.8 ms, typing p50
  1.7–2.5 ms, max 3.4–5.2 ms at 1× and 2×; plain StyledEdit as before.
  Checked in light and dark at 1×, 1.5× and 2× (review clean),
  through a reload.
  Since: a link's menu opens it (Open Link: a file from the document's
  folder, a URL by what opens it); Tab and ⇧Tab over code's selected
  lines indent and outdent them.
  Then: a table's columns aligned as its `:---:` line says; printed
  or exported (PDF, Word, OpenDocument, RTF, HTML) a Markdown document
